frame.situation:
Decision year 2050, round 4 of dash-2050-cons, the last round.

WHERE WE STAND
- We have launched nothing in rounds 1-3 and are on today's products.
- The 737 MAX holds at 57 a month on the FAA-agreed gates: Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line, 684 a year. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Hold is the only rate_737 value offered.
- Net debt has been $0.0B since 2029 (2030 in stress) and holds to 2050 in base and stress.
- The 777X and the MAX 7/10 are long done. My conditions for the next airplane (debt repaired, developments finished) are met [BX-1305, B-2326, BX-1247].

PUBLIC RECORD
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 on CFM + PW + RR, and its ramp is completing. Airbus is on the A320 Alt plan and is extending its NGSA engine slot agreements with CFM and the Joint Venture.
- The P&W-RR Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036; CFM's ducted engine since 2041; CFM-Embraer since 2042 (open and not exclusive).
- No A350 Re-engine is on the record. Airbus says "The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus."
- Observed narrowbody delivery share: 29.9% in 2048 (543 aircraft) and 27.0% in 2049 (483 against Airbus's 1,306).

DO NOTHING (-0.83 / -0.93 / -0.83)
- S1 = rivals hold; S2 = Airbus launches an A350 Re-engine; S3 = risk case, Airbus Delay Tactics (covert). With no fps, S3 equals S1.
- Demand now sits below the line. MAX deliveries are 513 (2050), 388 (2053), 346 (2055) and 248 (2060), against 684 of capacity: 75%, 57%, 51% and 36% used. The waiting backlog is 0.
- Preference: 27.7% (2050), 16.0% (2060).
- Operating profit runs $0.66B (2050), $1.30B (2055) and $1.43B (2060) a year below the game baseline. FCF stays at $12.66B or more, and net debt is held. Value erodes; the balance sheet doesn't.

OBJECTIVES UNDER DO NOTHING
- Not met: the 50/50 split and incumbency (worst year 27.7%).
- Met: balance-sheet repair, kept in base and stress.
- Engine enabler: dual sources not met (the MAX flies CFM only), and no 2050 order can meet it, since the earliest fps EIS is 2057. Three narrowbody makers: met.

THE GRID AGAINST DO NOTHING (S1 / S2 / S3; my calc in work/r4_ceo_frame_calc.py)
- 787 Re-engine alone: +0.44 / -0.60 / +0.44. Best plan in S1 and S3.
- 10-year at Renton: -0.86 / -0.85 / -0.92. At the new site: -0.96 / -0.95 / -1.02.
- 10-year at Renton + Re-engine: -0.56 / -1.60 / -0.62. Best fps row in S1 and S3.
- 7-year at Renton: -1.73 / -1.73 / -1.81. It trails the 10-year by $0.87-0.89B alone (inside ε) and by $1.00-1.02B with the Re-engine.
- Via Embraer: -3.12 to -4.26. It trails the Solo 10-year by $2.45-2.56B in every column.
- Renton adds +0.10 on a 10-year or via Embraer fps and +0.13 to +0.14 on a 7-year. It adds nothing while the fps holds.

TREND OF THE 10-YEAR AT RENTON AGAINST DO NOTHING
- 2026 PV: -5.26 (2030), -4.29 (2035), -1.78 (2045), -0.86 (2050).
- Decision-year dollars: -$7.8B, -$10.5B, -$11.9B, -$9.4B.
- Five years of the clock (x0.607) would take 2045's -1.78 to -1.08. The actual is -0.86. So, net of the clock, the market moved +$0.22B our way: the first gain in four rounds. Jay projected -1.08 to -1.28; the grid beat that by $0.22-0.42B. That is evidence an estimate was wrong [BX-1319], and I want to know why.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. Are the KPIs stable? Yes, on the brief. Pope's seat to confirm, now at falling volume.
2. Are market, technology and our balance sheet all ready?
   - Boeing: yes. Net debt is $0.0B, and every 10-year row holds stress net debt at $0.0B.
   - Technology: yes. Codes 5, 6 and 7 give CFM + the Joint Venture, both mature by any EIS from 2057.
   - Market: closer, but no. The best stand-alone fps still loses $0.86B against Do Nothing. A tie isn't convergence [BX-1296, BX-1303].
3. What if certification takes longer than we think? S3 is Jay's slip leg, with a limit of -2.83.
   - Every Solo row passes: 7-year at the new site by only $0.05B; 10-year at Renton by $1.08B; rows with the Re-engine by $0.22-1.38B.
   - Every via Embraer row fails, by $1.18-1.47B.
   - I still want the full cost of a slip, taken once [BX-1318].
4. Is this doing less, better? Do Nothing is within ε of every Solo 10-year row and of the Re-engine, and it has the least to execute [BX-1239].

BOARD RISKS (its guidance, not red lines)
It would veto:
- launch_10yr at any site and in any combination. It fails Business case ($1.86-2.10B short of +$1B) and the market leg. At the new site, or with the Re-engine, it also fails Downside (S3 -1.02 to -1.16).
- launch_7yr, on Business case, Downside and Boeing ready. With the Re-engine it overlaps 5 years.
- launch_via_embraer: Rating first (S3 -4.01 to -4.30), Business case and Downside.
- re787: launch in any combination. Its best column is +0.44, below +$1B at any odds.
- any premium above $2B.
It approves holds, and Renton with Pope's wind-down result. It says a premium can't carry a launch, because its tests read the grid.

It wants in the package:
- the submitted row beside Do Nothing, and each Board item's default row;
- my expected column;
- Jay's buffer and Fundable results with numbers, including a ruling on stress peaks that fall after 2050;
- Pope's KPI, supplier and strain results, including the MAX lines at falling volume;
- my standing rulings;
- every premium logged, with forgone holds shown apart;
- the trend, Jay's account of the beat, the erosion to 2060, and a plain statement that no later round remains;
- no fps date.

- As advice, I would also want an S3 margin that absorbs doctrine's +3-year slip at full cost: about $1.2B or more, against $1.08B today.
- If Pope's seat or the Board shows that my reconstruction misreads the grid, I will re-run it. That covers the window effect, Airbus's post-2060 slack and the Renton ramp.
- If the CEO takes the objective premium on the 10-year at Renton, I don't veto: it passes the slip leg by $1.08B and is fundable. I would log the $0.86-0.92B premium and tell the Board plainly that it is a tie carried by the mission, not a case.
- My binding veto on the four via Embraer rows lifts only on the grid: their S3 would have to reach -2.83.

FOR THE 787 RE-ENGINE
- Odds alone cannot move it: even at zero odds it is +0.44, inside epsilon.
- I would bring it only on a grid where its clean-column value clears $1B and S2 stays inside -$1B.
- An A350 Re-engine on the record closes it under H3.

CONDITIONS ON MY NUMBERS
They hold barring:
- an A350 Re-engine on the public record;
- a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem;
- any change to the stress-case cash path in the brief.
My 30% odds are Low confidence. They move the Re-engine premium between $0 and $0.44B, never past the cap.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran the slip leg as the baseline. Do Nothing scores -0.83 in S3, so the limit is -2.83. Every Solo row passes; the 10-year at Renton by $1.08B. Every via Embraer row fails, by $1.18-1.47B, and under the team rule I veto those four. The 7-year passes by only $0.05-0.19B: one to six months of slip. That isn't a baseline. Its stress peaks fall after 2050, and I rule them not held: it isn't fundable.

On the beat, I'm resetting my estimate. I charged the lost lead as a market loss, but against Do Nothing it isn't one. Do Nothing loses a point a year too, so the fps climbs the same 11 points whenever it lands. The window also slid onto the 2060s replacement wave. Net of the clock that is +$0.22B. It's real on this board, but the gain stream would have to double to clear +$1B; nothing on this order sheet does that.

A tie isn't a case. Within ε, Do Nothing has the higher worst column (-0.93 against -1.78) and adds no penalty, against $19.1B. A three-year slip, costed once and in full, takes $0.74-1.22B, most or all of the buffer.

The Re-engine is worth +0.13 at my 30% odds. Hold it; I log $0.13B.

So we hold everything, and say plainly that no later round remains: no new airplane in this game. The balance sheet stays fully restored, barring an A350 Re-engine on the record or a change to the stress path.

tests.name: KPI gate for the Rate Increase (my veto) [doctrine]
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of 5 a month, at least 6 months apart, each after 2-3 months of stable KPIs and an FAA review. Supplier readiness is a hard gate.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 1. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and the board has no injects. rate_737: hold is the only value offered, so no Rate Increase is on the order sheet. My veto has nothing to act on, and H6 cannot engage. Confirmed.

Is 57 a month stable on the gates? 57 a month is our FAA-agreed capacity: Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line, 684 a year. The line ran at that rate for 13 years, delivering 684 a year from 2035 to 2047, with no problem on the record. Since 2048 it has built to demand, not to 57: 543 (2048), 483 (2049) and 513 (2050), about 45, 40 and 43 a month. The brief gives no KPI series, so this result rests on its no-live-problem record.

Advice on the public line, not binding: say 'capacity of 57 a month on the FAA-agreed gates; we build to demand, about 43 a month in 2050'. The bulletin shows 483 deliveries in 2049. 'Holding at 57 a month' reads as 684 a year, and the public table says otherwise.

tests.name: Stability at falling volume: the MAX lines under Do Nothing [doctrine plus inference]
tests.threshold: The lines stay stable on the six FAA-agreed KPIs (rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages, training, ticketing) as volume falls. Any adjustment runs on the same gates and in steps (doctrine's step is 5 a month, at least 6 months apart), never as a cliff. Customers get honest delivery dates.

tests.name: Supplier readiness at falling volume: LEAP-1B and fragile suppliers [doctrine]
tests.threshold: Supplier readiness is a hard gate: no live supply-chain problem, and engine and structures supply that covers the rate, whether it is rising or falling.
tests.numbers:
Answer to asks 1 and 2.

LEAP-1B: our call falls with deliveries, from 1,368 engines at 57 a month to 1,026 (2050), 776 (2053), 692 (2055) and 496 (2060).
- From the observed tables (narrowbody engines = 2 x deliveries x share), CFM delivered about 1,671 narrowbody engines in 2049 (46.7% of 3,578). Our call took 966 of them (58%), against 61% in 2044 and 2048.
- CFM's Airbus load is about 705 engines and falling as A320neo slots return to CFM.
- Verdict: still a watch item, and an easing one. The risk has turned from rationing to low volume at the supplier.
- CFM puts the LEAP fleet first, with kits and shop material ahead of the OE delivery rate (bulletin).
- Keep the allocation reviews running [BX-1264, BX-1325], and attribute nothing to Airbus before exposure [B-1923].

Fragile suppliers at falling volume: the brief names none. Doctrine's answer:
- keep the fragile or financially weak ones funded and producing at or above our rate, and let the strong ones burn down inventory [B-2330, BX-1243];
- keep production infrastructure and trained labour through low-rate production, to protect the health of the production system and the supply chain [B-1618];
- give every supplier the step-down skyline early, because 'suppliers' health and rate readiness will be critical' whenever rates change [B-1616].
This is the frame's cash for readiness.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery: Do Nothing and the 787 Re-engine (EIS 2055) [record, applied by inference; the slip prior is doctrine]
tests.threshold: The plan's EIS can be delivered as stated. Read the risk-case column (S3, Delay Tactics) and say how much of the plan's value depends on the nominal date.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 9.

Do Nothing has no EIS to deliver. With no fps, S3 equals S1 (-0.83), and the worst column is S2 (-0.93).

787 Re-engine: the item against hold is +0.44 / -0.60 / +0.44. S3 equals S1, because Delay Tactics act only from fps EIS. S2 is Airbus's move, not a delivery risk.

The board prices no Re-engine slip. Doctrine's prior for a major derivative is +2 years central (range +1 to +4). Shifting the S1 item at 10.5% (inference) gives +0.40 at a 1-year slip, +0.36 at 2 years and +0.30 at 4. It stays positive in S1 and S3 across the range, so at most about a third of its value rides on the nominal date.

Readiness:
- Engine: the GEnx upgrade route has been ready since 2033, which gives 22 years by a 2055 EIS, and GE says it will keep improving it. Durability comes first [BX-1298, B-2304].
- Charleston builds 100 a year (8.3 a month). A lone re-engined 787 gaining 1 pp a year from 2055 needs 108.5 a year (9.0 a month) in 2060, 117 (9.7) in 2065 and 134 (11.2) in 2075. That fits inside a footprint being doubled for rates in the teens [B-2336, BX-1317].
- Workforce: nothing is in development, so one derivative fits the one-at-a-time rule [B-0341].
Operations can deliver it. My hold rests on ε, not on an operations finding.

tests.name: Two-front strain: the 10-year fps with the 787 Re-engine, and any single launch [doctrine; board arithmetic]
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine overlap at most 2 years (H4). Strain = $3B x overlap / 5, with the fps window running from EIS-7 to EIS and the Re-engine window from EIS-5 to EIS. One major development at a time.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 3. Confirmed:
- A 2050 Re-engine (2050-55) with a 2050 10-year fps (window 2053-60) overlaps 2 years (2053-55), $1.2B undiscounted. That is H4-legal with no slack. A 1-year Re-engine slip makes it 3 years ($1.8B), and doctrine's 2-year central slip makes it 4 ($2.4B); either would breach H4.
- On the grid the pairing costs the Re-engine $0.14-0.15B in every column: it is worth +0.30 / -0.75 / +0.30 beside the 10-year, against +0.44 / -0.60 / +0.44 alone. The fps item beside it is -1.00 / -1.00 / -1.06, which breaks the Board's -$1B limit in S3.

tests.name: Two-front strain: the 7-year fps with the 787 Re-engine [doctrine; board arithmetic]
tests.threshold: Overlap at most 2 years (H4).
tests.numbers:
A 2050 7-year fps (window 2050-57) against a 2050 Re-engine (2050-55) overlaps 5 years: $3.0B undiscounted, against a 2-year cap. H4 bars it, and the row is struck if ordered.

tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 4.

Capacity passes. Nothing is in development (the MAX 7/10 entered service in 2026 and the 777X in 2027), so one major development fits [B-0341].

Workforce: by 2050 we will have run no major development for 23 years, and our last clean sheet entered service in 2011. In 2045 the ExCo ordered two non-public moves: a dedicated fps risk-reduction team kept warm [B-1593], and a funded hiring and transfer plan [B-1941, B-0729]. The board neither reports nor prices their status, so I cannot put a measured number on it. The plan stays a condition of any launch.

Timing: new-airplane R&D starts 5-6 years before first delivery and peaks 1-2 years before it [B-0373]. For a 2060 EIS, that means a start in about 2054-55 and a peak in 2058-59, so a 2050 launch would leave 4-5 years to rebuild. Talent remains a 'ruthless competition' [B-1835].

At falling MAX volume (the stability test above), the people question turns inward: keep trained labour through low-rate production [B-1618], and redeploy before releasing anyone.

Pass on capacity; the workforce condition stays open.

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP: fps via Embraer [record, applied by inference]
tests.threshold: Solo where Boeing owns the airframe IP. Via Embraer only if the partner adds capital, capacity or IP that Boeing lacks.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 7. Via Embraer trails the Solo 10-year by $2.45B in every column alone, and by $2.56B with the Re-engine.

CFM's Embraer partnership (ready since 2042) is CFM's own, open and not exclusive, and it gives Boeing no capital, capacity or IP. Capacity is not what we lack: we have 171-436 idle MAX slots a year to 2060. Solo passes; via Embraer fails.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand [one remark; inference]
tests.threshold: Back a Rate Increase only where it adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column.
tests.numbers:
No Rate Increase row is on this round's grid (it was a 2030-only lever), so there is nothing to score.

For the record, the rule now runs the other way: demand has sat below capacity every year since 2048. Under Do Nothing, 513 (2050), 346 (2055) and 248 (2060) are delivered against 684 of capacity, leaving 171-436 slots a year idle. No capacity addition is warranted. tests.name: Renton wind-down readiness for any launch (signed, conditional) [rules arithmetic plus doctrine]
tests.threshold: The Renton MAX wind-down follows the fps ramp and never leads it. The Everett North Line carries on at up to 15 a month (180 a year). Renton is chosen at least 3 years before EIS for the full $3.0B.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 5.

One correction to the frame: MAX demand above Everett's 180 a year is 166 in 2055 (346 - 180), not 133. It is 147 in 2056, 125 in 2057 and 68 in 2060.

For a 2050 10-year launch (EIS 2060): on a linear reading of the rules' ramp (0 at EIS to 50 a month four years on; inference), the fps builds about 75 aircraft in its first year and runs at 150 a year by EIS+1. It covers the 68 within about the first year (2061). The board already has the MAX top up what the fps cannot build while it ramps. The step-down ladder keeps at least one Renton MAX line building through 2060 (22 a month against 20.7 of demand), so the ladder does not lead the ramp either.

Renton adds +0.10 in every column on a 10-year or via Embraer row and +0.13 to +0.14 on a 7-year. A 2050 launch would choose it 10 years before EIS, so the full $3.0B is avoided.

I sign the result for any launch on three conditions:
1. The trigger is the ramp, not a date: on a slip, Renton's MAX lines run on.
2. No airplane is built at rate before certification [BX-1263, B-2228].
3. Renton is chosen at least 3 years before EIS.

The site has no effect while the fps holds, so new_site stays.

tests.name: Engine code, should an fps launch (EIS 2060) [doctrine plus inference]
tests.threshold: The engines named are ready and durable by EIS. Two sources where available. Certification never runs concurrent with production.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 6. The code is null this round, since nothing launches. My read for a launch:
- The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036 and in NGSA service since 2037: 24 years since readiness by a 2060 EIS. P&W and RR delivered about 1,907 narrowbody engines in 2049 (53.4% of 3,578).

- Both pass durability-first by a 2060 EIS on a public record that reports no durability problem. P&W says it will report durability by operating environment, hot and sandy included; CFM says it does not trade durability for fuel burn [BX-1298, B-2304].

Supply stability: Code 3 keeps sole-source exposure, which is today's LEAP-1B position [B-1449]. Codes 5, 6 and 7 give two sources (CFM + the Joint Venture). I prefer Code 7 to Code 3, with Code 3 as the fallback on any reported Joint Venture durability problem.

Pacing: certify one lead installation for EIS and the second as a follow-on before its production slots, so certification never runs concurrent with production [BX-1263, B-2343].

No 2050 order meets the 2050 dual-source enabler. Engine choice is not my veto ground.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
(1) The KPI veto would bind if a brief offered a Rate Increase while reporting a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Neither holds this round. At falling volume, a supplier exit or a KPI breach (training, traveled work, supplier shortages) on a step down would pause the ladder at that rate until it is fixed.
(2) On the fps, I would need a grid with the 10-year Solo more than ε ahead of Do Nothing in the expected column, inside Malave's buffer, and a confirmed, funded hiring and transfer plan. This is the last round, so no later grid exists. The only operations lever the board prices is Renton (+0.10), and it is already in the best row. Engines and Renton pass.
(3) Operations passes the 787 Re-engine on every test, so my hold rests on ε (+0.44 at best; 0.44 - 1.04p at odds p) and on the Board's +$1B bar. Only a grid putting it above +$1B would move me. Its unpriced value is that a 2050-55 derivative keeps a development team in work. I report that, but with no fps to follow on this board, it bridges to nothing.
(4) I would withdraw the Renton sign-off if a launch plan wound Renton's MAX lines down ahead of the fps ramp, or tied the wind-down to a date.
(5) A reported durability problem on the Joint Venture engine would move me to a CFM-led installation (Code 3), with the second source added only after its own test evidence.
ops.memo:
My record is Global Services, not Commercial Airplanes. KPI, supplier and strain results are doctrine; delivery, IP and cash are my 2022 rules, applied by inference.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery [BX-1331]. No problem is live and hold is the only rate order, so my KPI veto has nothing to act on. The new task is stability at falling volume: 513 deliveries in 2050, 388 in 2053 and 248 in 2060, against 684 of capacity. Step the build rate down in fives on the same six KPIs: 42 a month now, 37 then 32 in 2052, 27 about 2056, 22 about 2058. That builds 4,014 against demand of 3,962 over 2050-60, never a cliff. Three of our four lines carry 42; two carry 27. Fragile suppliers stay funded and above our rate. For the public line: we build about 43 a month; 57 is capacity.

Second, engineering capacity. A 2050 Re-engine overlaps a 10-year fps by 2 years ($1.2B) with no slack, and a 7-year by 5, barred. A lone 10-year at Renton passes KPIs, suppliers and strain. Its predictable-delivery failure is value and certification risk after 23 years without a major development.

And finally, disciplined profitable growth [BX-1327]. The 10-year beats the 7-year by $0.87-0.93B. Embraer trails Solo by $2.45-2.56B and adds no IP we lack [BX-1330]. Renton's wind-down is signed on my three conditions. But no fps beats Do Nothing; the best trails by $0.86B. Hold on every lever, and run a smaller line well.

other_moves.move: Build the 737 MAX to demand on the FAA-agreed KPI gates; 57 a month is capacity, not the build rate
other_moves.detail: I'm correcting my own public line, on Pope's advice [BX-1284]. 57 a month is our capacity on the agreed gates: Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line, 684 a year. We have built to demand since 2048: 543 (2048), 483 (2049) and about 513 (2050), roughly 43 a month. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and hold is the only rate_737 order. Customers get honest delivery dates [BX-1274, BX-1259, BX-1271].

other_moves.move: Step the MAX build rate down with demand on the same six KPIs, and consolidate lines one at a time
other_moves.detail:
This is Pope's ladder (inference), in steps of 5 at least 6 months apart: 42 a month in 2050-51; 37 then 32 in 2052; 32 to 2055; 27 from about 2056; 22 from about 2058. Over 2050-60 it builds 4,014 aircraft against demand of 3,962, and the running gap stays under two months of output. Four steps in about six years, never a cliff [BX-1310].
- Each step is taken on rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages, training and ticketing. If a KPI degrades on a step, we hold that rate and fix it before the next one.
- Lines are consolidated one at a time. Which line goes is a KPI call, not a date.
- No target is published ahead of stability [BX-1268]. The board doesn't price this move.

other_moves.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot through the downturn; give the supply chain the step-down skyline early; LEAP-1B allocation reviews continue
other_moves.detail:
Cash for readiness [BX-1243, B-2330]. Fragile or financially weak suppliers stay funded and producing at or above our rate, while strong ones burn down inventory. Every supplier gets the step-down skyline within the planning window [B-1616].

LEAP-1B is still a watch item, and an easing one. Our call falls from about 1,026 engines (2050) to 496 (2060), so the risk has turned from rationing to low volume at the supplier. CFM's own LEAP fleet-support priority stands. Nothing is attributed to anyone before exposure [BX-1264, BX-1325].

other_moves.move: Keep trained labour through low-rate production; redeploy before releasing anyone
other_moves.detail: This protects the production system and the supply chain at falling volume [B-1618]. People on lines being consolidated move first to Everett, the 787 at Charleston, Defense, or the fps risk-reduction team.

other_moves.move: Keep improving the 787 and growing Charleston; keep bringing the GEnx upgrade to 787 customers with GE
other_moves.detail: Widebody growth comes from Charleston capacity on today's 787 [BX-1317, B-2336]. The GEnx upgrade is GE's own programme, ready since 2033, and durability comes first [BX-1298]. This is not a 787 Re-engine order, and the board doesn't price it.

other_moves.move: Put the 2050 fps case on the record as tested, and keep the risk-reduction team and the hiring and transfer plan warm; launch nothing
other_moves.detail:
THE CASE AS TESTED
- 10-year at Renton, Code 7 (CFM + the P&W-RR Joint Venture, two sources), with Code 3 as the fallback if a Joint Venture durability problem is reported.
- Pope's signed, conditional Renton wind-down.
- Cost-plus or risk-share terms, never fixed price [BX-1262, BX-1304].
- Against Do Nothing: -0.86 / -0.85 / -0.92.

THE TREND AGAINST DO NOTHING
- 2026 PV: -5.26 (2030), -4.29 (2035), -1.78 (2045), -0.86 (2050).
- Decision-year dollars: -$7.8B, -$10.5B, -$11.9B, -$9.4B.

MALAVE'S RESET, OWNED [BX-1319]: the lost lead isn't a loss against Do Nothing, and the 20-year window slid onto the 2060s replacement wave. Net of the clock that is +$0.22B, real on this board. The gain stream would still have to double ($3.66B PV against $1.80B) to clear +$1B.

No later round remains on this board, so this hold means no new airplane in this game. The team and the funded hiring and transfer plan [B-1941, B-0729, B-1593] stay because readiness doesn't keep by itself, not as a bridge to a dated launch. No date [B-2315].

decision.public_statement:
I've said for a long time that we'll do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. That's still the test, and I owe you a straight read on it.

We're ready on our end. The factories are stable. The 777X and the MAX 7 and 10 have been flying with customers for years. The balance sheet is where it should be. The technology is ready too: there are good, mature engines out there from more than one maker. The market case for our next airplane moved our way this year, for the first time in a while. I think it's turning. I don't think it's turned. So we're not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date for one. I'd rather tell you plainly that the case isn't there than launch an airplane to avoid saying so. Another company's schedule doesn't set ours.

When we do launch, you'll get an entry-into-service date we know we can meet, with room built into it. We'll share the development risk sensibly with our partners, and we won't take a fixed-price bet on it.

One correction from me on the 737. I've been saying we're holding at 57 a month. That's our capacity, on the gates we agreed with the FAA. We build to demand, and this year that's about 43 a month. As demand comes down, we'll bring the rate down in steps on those same gates, never off a cliff, and we'll keep our suppliers and our people ready through it. Customers will keep getting honest delivery dates.

On widebodies, the 787 is the most efficient airplane in its class. We'll keep making it better with our partners at GE, and we'll keep investing in Charleston.

We'd rather do fewer things and do them well. The financials will follow our production performance.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing in every field.
- Orders: fps hold, fps_engine_code null, fps_site new_site, rate_737 hold, re787 hold.
- Every order is the default, so no item goes to the Board.
- No veto stands against the plan, and I take no override.

THE TEAM RULE, APPLIED
(1) Malave's buffer test, the binding check. S3 must be no lower than -2.83 (Do Nothing's -0.83 less $2B).
- Do Nothing: -0.83, $2.00B clear.
- Every Solo row passes. The 10-year at Renton clears by $1.08B; the 7-year by only $0.05-0.19B.
- Every via Embraer row fails, by $1.18-1.47B. Jay's veto on those four binds. None is ordered.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS

Expected column: S1, the narrowbody's planning column, with the Re-engine blended at Jay's 30%.
- Do Nothing -0.86; 10-year at Renton -1.72 (-0.86 against Do Nothing); 10-year at Renton + Re-engine -1.73 (-0.87).

- Via Embraer is barred by Jay's veto, trails Solo by $2.45-2.56B in every column and, on Pope's IP test, adds nothing we lack.

THE LAST ROUND, PLAINLY
No later round remains on this board, so this hold means no new airplane in this game. I say that rather than launch to avoid saying it. The Board asked for that, and it's my own standard [BX-1241, BX-1322]. The trend did turn, for the first time:

Jay owned his miss [BX-1319]. Against Do Nothing, the lost lead isn't a loss, because Do Nothing also loses a point a year; and the window slid onto the 2060s replacement wave. "I think that we're turning it. I don't think it's turned" [BX-1300]. The gain stream would have to double to clear +$1B.

Value erodes; the balance sheet doesn't.

STANDING RULINGS

COSTS AND BIASES

final.public_statement:
I've said for a long time that we'll do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. That's still the test, and I owe you a straight read on it.

We're ready on our end. The factories are stable. The 777X and the MAX 7 and 10 have been flying with customers for years. The balance sheet is where it should be. The technology is ready too: there are good, mature engines out there from more than one maker. The market case for our next airplane moved our way this year, for the first time in a while. I think it's turning. I don't think it's turned. So we're not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date for one. I'd rather tell you plainly that the case isn't there than launch an airplane to avoid saying so. Another company's schedule doesn't set ours.

When we do launch, you'll get an entry-into-service date we know we can meet, with room built into it. We'll share the development risk sensibly with our partners, and we won't take a fixed-price bet on it.

One correction from me on the 737. I've been saying we're holding at 57 a month. That's our capacity, on the gates we agreed with the FAA. We build to demand, and this year that's about 43 a month. As demand comes down, we'll bring the rate down in steps on those same gates, never off a cliff, and we'll keep our suppliers and our people ready through it. Customers will keep getting honest delivery dates.

On widebodies, the 787 is the most efficient airplane in its class. We'll keep making it better with our partners at GE, and we'll keep investing in Charleston.

We'd rather do fewer things and do them well. The financials will follow our production performance.

DECISION: Do Nothing in every field.
- Orders: fps hold, fps_engine_code null, fps_site new_site, rate_737 hold, re787 hold.
- Every order is the default, so no item goes to the Board.
- No veto stands against the plan, and I take no override.

THE TEAM RULE, APPLIED
(1) Malave's buffer test, the binding check. S3 must be no lower than -2.83 (Do Nothing's -0.83 less $2B).
- Do Nothing: -0.83, $2.00B clear.

- Every via Embraer row fails, by $1.18-1.47B. Jay's veto on those four binds. None is ordered.
(2) Pope's KPI veto: nothing to bind on. No Rate Increase is offered, and the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. H6 is not engaged.
(3) Everything else is my call. Within ε, doing less [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] break the tie.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. Are the KPIs stable? Yes: Pope's KPI and supplier tests pass. The new task is stability at falling volume, handled in other moves.
2. Are market, technology and our balance sheet all ready? [BX-1296, BX-1305]
- Balance sheet: yes. Net debt is $0.0B since 2029, held in base and stress. Every 10-year row is fundable ($0.0B stress peak).
- Technology: yes. The Joint Venture engine would have 24 years since readiness by a 2060 EIS, and CFM's ducted engine 19.
- Market: no. The best stand-alone fps, the 10-year at Renton, is -0.86 / -0.85 / -0.92 against Do Nothing. The three streams haven't converged.
3. What if certification takes longer? Jay costed doctrine's +3-year slip once and in full: $0.74-1.22B against a $1.08B margin. It absorbs the slip on the narrow count only.
- Pope fails the 10-year on predictable delivery: value at the nominal date, certification pacing, and 23 years without a major development.
- She is clear it is not a KPI, supplier or strain failure.
4. Is this doing less, better? Yes. Do Nothing is within ε of every Solo 10-year row and of the Re-engine, and it has the least to execute.

THE NARROWBODY
Expected column: S1, the narrowbody's planning column, with the Re-engine blended at Jay's 30%.
- Do Nothing -0.86; 10-year at Renton -1.72 (-0.86 against Do Nothing); 10-year at Renton + Re-engine -1.73 (-0.87).
My debt-first test fails: it needs a plan more than ε ahead. Doctrine's last-round rule (profile §6: launch only if the fps beats Do Nothing by more than ε) fails too; that rule is doctrine, not my record. The tie breaks to Do Nothing on four counts:
- less to execute;
- the higher worst column (-0.93 against -1.78);
- no added penalty ($19.1B undiscounted, for scale only; the grid already nets it);
- the higher-confidence plan.
The Board would veto any launch on Business case ($1.86B short of +$1B), so an order would revert to hold anyway.
- The 7-year trails the 10-year by $0.87-0.89B, fails Fundable under Jay's ruling (a stress peak of $1.0-6.4B after 2050 counts as not held) and has thin buffer margins.
- Via Embraer is barred by Jay's veto, trails Solo by $2.45-2.56B in every column and, on Pope's IP test, adds nothing we lack.

THE LAST ROUND, PLAINLY
No later round remains on this board, so this hold means no new airplane in this game. I say that rather than launch to avoid saying it. The Board asked for that, and it's my own standard [BX-1241, BX-1322]. The trend did turn, for the first time:
- 2026 PV: -5.26 (2030), -4.29 (2035), -1.78 (2045), -0.86 (2050);
- decision-year dollars: -$11.9B (2045) to -$9.4B (2050);
- the market moved +$0.22B our way net of the clock.
Jay owned his miss [BX-1319]. Against Do Nothing, the lost lead isn't a loss, because Do Nothing also loses a point a year; and the window slid onto the 2060s replacement wave. "I think that we're turning it. I don't think it's turned" [BX-1300]. The gain stream would have to double to clear +$1B.

Do Nothing erosion, on the record:
- preference 27.7% (2050) to 16.0% (2060);
- operating profit $0.66B (2050), $1.30B (2055) and $1.43B (2060) a year below the game baseline;
- FCF $12.66B or more, and net debt held.
Value erodes; the balance sheet doesn't.

THE 787 RE-ENGINE: HOLD
Item value against hold is 0.44 - 1.04p. At Jay's 30% (Low confidence) that is +0.13; break-even is 42%, and it is never above ε, even at zero odds.
- Tie-breakers: the higher worst column (-0.93 against -1.53), doing less, and no added $0.6B penalty.
- The Board vetoes it on Business case.

STANDING RULINGS
- H1: stays lifted. The 777X has been in service since 2027 and the MAX 7/10 since 2026; debt was repaired in 2029 [BX-0550, BX-1299, BX-1305, B-2326].

- H5: nothing to cancel.

MY RED LINES, ALL KEPT

- no fixed-price development;
- no blame on the FAA;
- no supplier problem attributed to Airbus.

COSTS AND BIASES
On the grid the decision costs nothing: Do Nothing is the best plan in S2 and inside ε of the best in S1 and S3. Two biases show, both at no cost. Under-disclosure: the step-down ladder isn't published. Cash for readiness: suppliers are kept funded at falling volume.

LEAN: the all-default package (ngsa hold, engine code fixed, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt), with no Board item. The A350's Do Nothing goes on the record as a final, deliberate choice.

ORDER OF ARGUMENT
- Five pillars first [AX-0073, AX-0081]. NGSA is at full rate and the in-service A320 fleet is flying without its lines. Nothing goes on top of that which Lars cannot pass. No engine enters service before it is mature: on the record, no widebody engine for the A350 is committed for a 2055 EIS.
- Ramp: disciplined and controlled to the last step [AX-0010]. It is complete, and we keep it that way.
- Prepare the next decade. NGSA is in service and paid for. A late, cheap A350 derivative is one I would welcome [AX-0082, A-0090], but not ahead of its engine. The generation after NGSA stays on its own technology clock, inside R&D, with no launch implied [AX-0020, AX-0006].
- What I can take to the Board.
  - My rule takes the company default when it is within $1B of the best plan. Doctrine launches the A350 Re-engine only on at least $1B over Do Nothing (profile section 6). The Re-engine adds +0.57 in S1-S5 (+0.47 weighted) and loses 0.42 in S6 / S7, so it clears neither bar.
  - Unlike in 2045, its worst column (+13.64) is now below the default's (+14.06).
  - The tie-breaks (less concurrency, a later capex start, fewer Board items) all point to hold.

WHAT THE LAST ROUND CHANGES, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT
- There is no later round, so holding is Do Nothing on the A350 for good. I want the ExCo to decide that knowingly.
- The $1B band is a hurdle on the size of the gain, not a value-of-waiting test, so it does not fall away because the game ends. I have asked Thomas to confirm or correct this on the numbers.
- About $0.57B forgone in S1 ($0.47B weighted) is inside the band. It is not a doctrine premium.

HOW FIRMLY I HOLD THE LEAN
This is my rule, not a red line, and the Board has asked for this case three rounds running. So test the Re-engine in full, as if it were going to the Board: cash and the net-cash path, robustness, a mature engine for 2055, and absorption by milestone.
- If either of your tests fails, the hold stands. At +0.57 no override is possible, and the Board would veto one.
- If both pass cleanly, my own default test still decides at +0.57. I will record that as the ground, so that the A350's Do Nothing rests on our rule and not on a gap in the analysis.

NOT IN PLAY
- Delay Tactics stay off and are closed for the whole game. No fps is public. One move is -7.81 in S1 and S6 and negative in every other column. They fail rules 4 and 5 and integrity. The team's stricter condition was never set aside [A-0299, A-0474].

REACTION DISCIPLINE

- A 787 Re-engine made public triggers no other move.

EXPECTED SCENARIO
- S1, rivals hold. Boeing says the market case is 'not there yet' and that it would 'rather do fewer things'. On the widebody it is improving the current 787 with GE.
- Working weights are unchanged: S1 50%, S2 15%, S3 5%, S4 15%, S5 5%, S6 5%, S7 5%. Only S6 / S7 (10%) move our number.
- Weighted: default +14.09, Re-engine +14.56. The call does not turn on the scenario: the item keeps its sign unless a 787 Re-engine is more than about 58% likely.

PUBLIC LINE
- Five pillars first.

- The in-service A320 fleet fully supported.
- The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus and competes on product and value. No engine is named, and there is no Re-engine signal.
- The technologies for the next generation are prepared on the clock of maturity.
- Financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet.

- Windows, not dates. No payout figures. No Delay Tactics, so the staffing clause is struck.

cfo.memo:
Round 4 (2050), the last decision year. Recommended: ngsa hold, engine code none (fixed in service; I defer to Lars), rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt. No Board item.

Cash is not the obstacle. The A350 Re-engine costs $5B / 5 = $1.0B a year over 2050-54. NGSA spend ended in 2036 and the Alt plan's $0.75B is spent: no overlap, no strain. A peak of $1.0B against $5.228B (EUR 4,753m at $1.10) leaves $4.23B for all prepayments. Net cash at end-2054 (an inference), without / with the Re-engine: $118.4B / $113.4B at our 48% practice; $177.4B / $172.4B at 30%; $111.8B / $106.8B at 50%. No equity raise.

Robustness. Both rows stay positive in their worst column (default +14.06, Re-engine +13.64), so both pass the row test. The item is +0.57 in S1-S5 and -0.42 in S6 / S7, +0.47 weighted, inside the -$2B line. It never reaches $1B and turns negative in two plausible columns, so it fails the company's added-move test: a binding soft veto, not a red line.

The last round does not lower the bar. The $1B is a hurdle on the size of the gain and never contained a waiting term. In 2045 I pre-read a 2050 launch at +0.61, below $1B; the grid now shows +0.57. No override can pass at that margin.

Holding forgoes $0.47B weighted, for good, inside the band: a deliberate choice.

Delay Tactics are deleted: a naked $48.32B fine, rules 4 and 5.

tests.name: Safety: NGSA at full rate and the in-service A320 fleet after its lines closed [Faury ask 1]
tests.threshold: Five pillars. No order may compromise safety, and no override is possible. The Board accepts no override of this result.
tests.numbers:
The brief reports no safety event and no open finding.
- NGSA: 1,339 in 2050 (about 112 a month), 1,352 in 2051 and 1,344 in 2052, then 1,298 (2053) and 1,284 (2054) against capacity of 1,366 (about 114 a month) from 2053. The line is in its fourteenth year of service, there is no waiting backlog, and nothing calls for a rate above plan.
- A320: the lines closed in 2047 and the in-service fleet keeps flying. The CFM LEAP and P&W GTF Advantage aftermarket programmes are public and run fleet first.
Passes on the default row and on the Re-engine row.

tests.name: Quality and public explanation [Faury asks 1 and 7]
tests.threshold: No order, other move or statement line whose public explanation would contradict safety and quality.

tests.numbers:
The end-2027 rate commitment closed long ago, and the A320 lines have been shut since 2047. A320neo engine slots have not been needed since 2047, and the surplus has gone back to CFM and P&W.

On the Re-engine row, a widebody development in 2050-54 draws on the A350 and design teams, not on A320 sustaining engineering. NGSA development ended in 2036-37, and A320 line staff were freed from 2047.

Condition on both rows: no A320 sustaining or NGSA in-service support staff are moved to staff a derivative [A-0366, A-0485].

Passes on both rows.

tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply-chain crunch, there is no new concurrency and the A350 Re-engine waits (profile section 5, row 12). The Board accepts no override of this result.

tests.threshold: NGSA / A350 development overlap of 2 years or less ($1.2B strain), unless the grid shows at least $1B more. At most one new launch per round. A failure is also a red line.

NGSA was developed in 2030-37 (spend ended in 2036). The Re-engine would be developed in 2050-55, with EIS in 2055.
- Overlap: 0 years, so strain is $3B x 0 / 5 = $0.
- It would be the only launch this round.

NGSA in-service support and the steps from 1,339 to 1,366 a year are sustaining work, not development.

The test passes, so there is nothing to bind.

tests.name: A350F and Spirit A350 absorption, shown by a milestone [Faury ask 5]
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 work packages are still being absorbed. The proxy (round 2 at the earliest) is met, and Faury asked for a milestone.
tests.numbers:
Starting point, both in 2025, 25 years before 2050:
- the A350F entered its industrial phase;
- the Spirit A350 work packages were taken in-house.

Milestone: the A350 family delivered 70 a year (41.2% of 170) in each of the 24 years 2026-2049, and no bulletin reports an A350F, Spirit, quality or supply event.

Limits:
- The sources hold no dated A350F EIS or Spirit close-out, because the evidence ends in early 2026.
- The board sets widebody deliveries from its share rule (41.2% x 170). A steady 70 a year is therefore what it would show with or without a production problem. The real evidence is that no event was reported in 24 years.
- A steady rate shows the work was absorbed. It does not show spare engineering capacity.

tests.name: Production readiness: the A350 Re-engine airframe and the A350 lines [Faury ask 6]
tests.threshold: The A350 lines can take a Re-engine and its ramp without destabilising the line.
tests.numbers:
The line has been stable at 70 a year (about 6 a month) for 24 years. A Re-engine is a derivative, as the A330neo was: a new engine, nacelle and pylon.

Alone (S1-S5), the A350 gains 1.5 pp a year from 41.2% to 60%. That takes about 12.5 years, so deliveries rise from 70 to about 102 a year, about +2.6 a year. That is a gentle ramp.

In S6 / S7 the share stays flat at 70 a year.

The airframe side passes. The engine side does not (next test).

tests.name: Production readiness: a mature widebody engine for a 2055 EIS [Faury ask 4; Board question]
tests.threshold:
Readiness is proven before launch.
- Team Step 3: the Re-engine's engine adds 0 EIS years, and any engine that adds years needs at least $1B.
- Doctrine (profile section 11.3): the UltraFan widebody is committed a year before our A350 launch.
- Rule 8 note: the A350 Re-engine defaults to Rolls-Royce.
A failure is a soft veto.
tests.numbers:
WHAT CHANGED SINCE 2045: nothing on the engine. No UltraFan widebody, A350 Trent upgrade or other widebody engine for the A350 has been launched or committed.

CANDIDATES FOR A 2055 EIS:
- UltraFan widebody: ready launch + 6. If Rolls-Royce launched it blind this round, it would be ready in 2056, a year after a 2055 EIS. On Rolls-Royce's own sequence (its board acts only in the round a Re-engine is on the record), it would come after this round, and no round is left. Either way it is not mature for 2055.
- GEnx upgrade (ready since 2033) and Trent 1000 upgrade: both are 787 engines. Neither has flown on the A350 or been offered for it.
- Trent XWB: today's engine. Rolls-Royce's durability work inside its existing budget is not a Re-engine.
- CFM RISE: technology only, with no product and no date.

ANSWER: a 2055 Re-engine has no named engine and no mature one. The EIS must move to 2056 at the earliest. Since no engine is committed, it would in fact move to an undated year.

VALUE (pure discount at 8%, my inference):
- re-timed to 2056: +0.53 in S1-S5, -0.39 in S6 / S7, about +0.44 weighted;
- re-timed to 2057: about +0.49.
An engine that adds EIS years needs at least $1B under Step 3. None of these reaches it.

CONSISTENCY WITH 2045: in 2045 I wrote that moving the EIS to the engine's year would pass readiness. That assumed an engine on the record with a year to move to. None exists, and Step 3's $1B for an added EIS year still applies.

RESULT: fail, a soft veto, binding. Grid margin against the best passing option (the all-default row):
- +0.57 in S1-S5;
- -0.42 in S6 / S7;
- +0.47 weighted.
That is below $1B, so no override can carry it.

The last round does not lower this test. Readiness is a precondition on the engine, not a value-of-waiting test, and if anything it has hardened: in 2045 an engine could still have been committed in time; now none can.

tests.name: Five pillars: engine maturity, no immature engine enters service [Faury ask 4]

tests.numbers:
This is a re-timing note, not a breach, on two conditions: the case states that the EIS moves to the engine's maturity, and no engine is named in public. The hold row meets both trivially.

A Re-engine case submitted at the grid's 2055 EIS (the +14.66 row as dated) with no mature engine would breach this pillar. That would be binding, and the Board lists it as a veto ground.

The hold rests on my readiness soft veto above, not on a pillars breach.

tests.numbers:

Rule checks:

- Rule 5 fails on the hold row, since nothing is in development. On the Re-engine row a programme would be in development, but rule 4 alone deletes the move.
- Integrity bars bottleneck and both.

The team's stricter condition stands and has never been set aside. Deleted.

SIZING
- NGSA engine slots with CFM and the Joint Venture: 2,568-2,732 a year (deliveries of 1,284-1,352, capacity of 1,366), below the 2,770 of 2044.

'Engineering staffing for NGSA in-service support and sustaining: we fill these roles by internal redeployment first, including former A320 line staff, and then by normal hiring. A320 sustaining engineering for the in-service fleet and the A350 teams stay fully staffed. The staffing is sized to our own programmes and does not target any competitor's programme or staff.'

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Toward a pass on the Re-engine:
- **An A350 widebody engine on the public record before submission, mature by the Re-engine's EIS.** Examples are a committed UltraFan widebody or an A350 Trent upgrade with a ready year at or before 2055. This is the last round and no bulletin comes before sealed orders, so it cannot happen in this game.
- **A non-default engine with a real certification path.** For example, CFM/GE offers its mature GEnx upgrade for the A350 with certification inside the five-year development. My engine test would pass on maturity, but Step 3 would still ask for at least $1B.
- **An engine-paced EIS that clears Step 3.** That means the EIS moves to a committed engine's year and the re-timed item still shows at least $1B. On the brief it shows about +0.53.

If the engine were secured, I would see no operating reason to hold: zero overlap, NGSA at full rate, and A320 staff freed. The within-$1B rule would then be for Faury and Toepfer.

Toward more caution:
- a reported supply crunch on the NGSA engine chain (2,568-2,732 engines a year), structures, titanium or rare earths;
- an adverse Joint Venture durability finding;
- a quality escape or safety event on NGSA or the in-service A320 fleet.
Any of these fails more tests and freezes new concurrency.

A 787 Re-engine on the record closes the A350 Re-engine under rule 3.

Delay Tactics: nothing in this round reopens them.
ops.memo:
My tests come from my role, not my record. Confidence: Very low.

The base passes. NGSA builds 1,339 aircraft in 2050 on CFM and the Joint Venture, with capacity of 1,366 from 2053. That needs 2,568-2,732 engines a year, below the 2,770 we carried in 2044 without a crunch. The A320 lines are closed, and sustaining engineering for the in-service fleet stays fully staffed. Safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch pass on both rows. The Joint Venture's durability is a watch item, not a constraint.

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is at full rate, and we run it in a disciplined and controlled way. It flies on robust, multi-source engine supply from CFM and from the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, and we will report its in-service performance as the fleet data show it. We brought it into service on the clock of maturity, and that is the clock we keep. A320 family production has completed, and we keep the in-service fleet fully supported, with its sustaining engineering fully staffed. We are securing the engines, structures and materials our own production needs, on standard terms. The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus and competes on product and value. We keep preparing the technologies for the generation after this one, on the clock of their maturity. We continue to fund our programmes from our own cash generation, within our financial framework, and to preserve our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. Together with our European industrial base, our suppliers and our partners worldwide, we will continue to work with the whole industry for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aviation.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: the all-default package. ngsa hold, engine code fixed (none), rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt. There is no Board item. The A350's Do Nothing is recorded as a final, deliberate choice.

ORDER OF ARGUMENT
1. Five pillars [AX-0073, AX-0081]. NGSA is at full rate, and the in-service A320 fleet flies without its lines. Wagner passes safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch on both rows, and no event is reported. One condition binds any A350 case: no engine enters service before it is mature. No widebody engine for the A350 is launched or committed. A case dated at the grid's 2055 EIS would breach the pillar; one that moves the EIS would carry a re-timing note.
2. Ramp. It is complete, disciplined and controlled [AX-0010], and nothing goes on top of it that Wagner cannot pass.
3. Prepare the next decade. NGSA is in service and paid for. The generation after it stays on its technology clock, inside R&D, with no launch implied [AX-0020, AX-0006].
4. What I can take to the Board. Nothing beyond the default on this round's tests.

STEP 1: DELETE RED-LINE AND PILLAR BREACHES
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted.
  - Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked against the $48.32B fine.
  - Rule 5: nothing is in development.
  - 'both' is a second move.
  - Bottleneck and both fail integrity.
  - Each item is negative in every column: one move -7.81 / -0.14 / -0.14 / -0.15 / -0.14 / -7.81 / -0.14; both moves -7.99 to -0.27. S1 and S6 break the -$2B line.
- A Re-engine case submitted at a 2055 EIS with no mature engine would breach the pillars (Wagner). So the only Re-engine case that could even be tested is one that moves the EIS to a mature engine. No such engine exists on the record.
- Rule 3 is open (no 787 Re-engine is on the record; GEnx is 'not a 787 Re-engine order'), and rule 6 is clean (zero overlap, one launch). Neither binds.

STEP 2: SURVIVORS
- The default passes every test of Toepfer and Wagner.
- The A350 Re-engine fails two binding soft vetoes, on independent grounds:
  - Toepfer: the added-move test. The item is +0.57 in S1-S5 and -0.42 in S6 / S7 (+0.47 at my weights). It never reaches $1B and turns negative in two plausible columns. It passes cash ($1.0B a year, $4.23B of headroom), the row test (worst column +13.64), the -$2B line and rule 6.
  - Wagner: engine readiness. Nothing has changed since 2045. An UltraFan widebody launched blind now would be ready in 2056. On Rolls-Royce's own sequence it comes only after a Re-engine is on the record, and no round is left. The GEnx and Trent 1000 upgrades are 787 engines. Re-timed, the item is about +0.53 (2056) or +0.49 (2057), still short of the $1B that an added EIS year needs (team Step 3).
- So the only survivor is the default.

STEP 3: CHOOSE
- The raw best in my expected scenario (S1) is the Re-engine at +14.66, against the default's +14.09: a gap of +0.57 (+0.47 weighted). That is inside the $1B band where my rule takes the company default (profile section 9, step 6). It also falls short of doctrine's own $1B launch condition for the A350 Re-engine (profile section 6).
- Unlike in 2045, robustness now also favours hold. The Re-engine row's worst column (+13.64) trails the default's (+14.06) by $0.42B.
- All the tie-breaks point to hold:
  - less concurrency;
  - a later capex start (none, against $1.0B a year from 2050);
  - fewer Board items (0 against 1 Qualified Majority item).
- Three grounds lead to hold, each on its own: Toepfer's veto, Wagner's veto and my default rule.

THE LAST ROUND
I put the Board's question to both colleagues.
- Toepfer confirms on the numbers that the $1B is a hurdle on the size of the gain. It never contained a waiting term, so the last round does not lower it. He applied it in 2045 to a launch-now item, and his 2045 pre-read of a 2050 launch (+0.61, held under the same test) is borne out at +0.57.
- Wagner confirms that readiness is a precondition on the engine, not a value-of-waiting test, and that it has hardened: in 2045 an engine could still have been committed in time, and now none can.
Irreversibility cuts both ways: a hold cannot be reversed, and a launch could not be cancelled before 2055. I decide the hold knowingly, as the A350's final Do Nothing.

OVERRIDE CHECK
None is used. An override needs at least $1B over the best passing option. The Re-engine is +0.57 at best and trails by $0.42B in the worst column, and the Board would veto a Re-engine reached by override. My one override per game ends the game unused.

WHAT I ACCEPT, KNOWINGLY
I forgo about $0.57B in S1 ($0.47B weighted), for good. That is inside the band, so it is not a doctrine premium. The A350 stays at 70 a year and 41.2% share on the grid, competing on product and price, as older widebodies have before [A-0090, A-0091]. Its single engine source (Trent XWB) becomes a standing watch.

BOARD-GATE LINES
- Package: no Board item. Every field is at its default.
- For the record, the Re-engine not submitted:
  - Pillars: pass only if its EIS moves; a 2055-dated case would breach them.
  - Toepfer: fail on the added-move test (binding soft veto); cash passes.
  - Wagner: fail on engine readiness (binding soft veto); safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch pass.
  - Grid item: +0.57 x5 / -0.42 x2.
  - Not taken to the Board, since the Board's first condition (both pass, no override) is not met.

REACTION DISCIPLINE (rules 2 and 7)
- An fps launched now enters service in 2057 or later and needs no reply.
- NGSA is never cancelled.
- No Re-engine is approved, so a same-round 787 Re-engine triggers nothing.

DELAY TACTICS
Off for the whole game: none was ordered in any round from 2030 to 2050. The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) was never set aside, and I do not set it aside now. They are never named in public: the 2045 staffing clause is struck.

CONFIDENCE
My decision style is rated Low in the profile. Toepfer's and Wagner's tests are role-derived (Low and Very low).

final.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is at full rate, and we run it in a disciplined and controlled way. It flies on robust, multi-source engine supply from CFM and from the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, and we will report its in-service performance as the fleet data show it. We brought it into service on the clock of maturity, and that is the clock we keep. A320 family production has completed, and we keep the in-service fleet fully supported, with its sustaining engineering fully staffed. We are securing the engines, structures and materials our own production needs, on standard terms. The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus and competes on product and value. We keep preparing the technologies for the generation after this one, on the clock of their maturity. We continue to fund our programmes from our own cash generation, within our financial framework, and to preserve our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. Together with our European industrial base, our suppliers and our partners worldwide, we will continue to work with the whole industry for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aviation.
final.rationale:
DECISION: the all-default package. ngsa hold, engine code fixed (none), rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt. There is no Board item. The A350's Do Nothing is recorded as a final, deliberate choice.

ORDER OF ARGUMENT
1. Five pillars [AX-0073, AX-0081]. NGSA is at full rate, and the in-service A320 fleet flies without its lines. Wagner passes safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch on both rows, and no event is reported. One condition binds any A350 case: no engine enters service before it is mature. No widebody engine for the A350 is launched or committed. A case dated at the grid's 2055 EIS would breach the pillar; one that moves the EIS would carry a re-timing note.
2. Ramp. It is complete, disciplined and controlled [AX-0010], and nothing goes on top of it that Wagner cannot pass.
3. Prepare the next decade. NGSA is in service and paid for. The generation after it stays on its technology clock, inside R&D, with no launch implied [AX-0020, AX-0006].
4. What I can take to the Board. Nothing beyond the default on this round's tests.

STEP 1: DELETE RED-LINE AND PILLAR BREACHES
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted.
  - Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked against the $48.32B fine.
  - Rule 5: nothing is in development.
  - 'both' is a second move.
  - Bottleneck and both fail integrity.
  - Each item is negative in every column: one move -7.81 / -0.14 / -0.14 / -0.15 / -0.14 / -7.81 / -0.14; both moves -7.99 to -0.27. S1 and S6 break the -$2B line.
- A Re-engine case submitted at a 2055 EIS with no mature engine would breach the pillars (Wagner). So the only Re-engine case that could even be tested is one that moves the EIS to a mature engine. No such engine exists on the record.
- Rule 3 is open (no 787 Re-engine is on the record; GEnx is 'not a 787 Re-engine order'), and rule 6 is clean (zero overlap, one launch). Neither binds.

STEP 2: SURVIVORS
- The default passes every test of Toepfer and Wagner.
- The A350 Re-engine fails two binding soft vetoes, on independent grounds:
  - Toepfer: the added-move test. The item is +0.57 in S1-S5 and -0.42 in S6 / S7 (+0.47 at my weights). It never reaches $1B and turns negative in two plausible columns. It passes cash ($1.0B a year, $4.23B of headroom), the row test (worst column +13.64), the -$2B line and rule 6.
  - Wagner: engine readiness. Nothing has changed since 2045. An UltraFan widebody launched blind now would be ready in 2056. On Rolls-Royce's own sequence it comes only after a Re-engine is on the record, and no round is left. The GEnx and Trent 1000 upgrades are 787 engines. Re-timed, the item is about +0.53 (2056) or +0.49 (2057), still short of the $1B that an added EIS year needs (team Step 3).
- So the only survivor is the default.

STEP 3: CHOOSE
- The raw best in my expected scenario (S1) is the Re-engine at +14.66, against the default's +14.09: a gap of +0.57 (+0.47 weighted). That is inside the $1B band where my rule takes the company default (profile section 9, step 6). It also falls short of doctrine's own $1B launch condition for the A350 Re-engine (profile section 6).
- Unlike in 2045, robustness now also favours hold. The Re-engine row's worst column (+13.64) trails the default's (+14.06) by $0.42B.
- All the tie-breaks point to hold:
  - less concurrency;
  - a later capex start (none, against $1.0B a year from 2050);
  - fewer Board items (0 against 1 Qualified Majority item).
- Three grounds lead to hold, each on its own: Toepfer's veto, Wagner's veto and my default rule.

THE LAST ROUND
I put the Board's question to both colleagues.
- Toepfer confirms on the numbers that the $1B is a hurdle on the size of the gain. It never contained a waiting term, so the last round does not lower it. He applied it in 2045 to a launch-now item, and his 2045 pre-read of a 2050 launch (+0.61, held under the same test) is borne out at +0.57.
- Wagner confirms that readiness is a precondition on the engine, not a value-of-waiting test, and that it has hardened: in 2045 an engine could still have been committed in time, and now none can.
Irreversibility cuts both ways: a hold cannot be reversed, and a launch could not be cancelled before 2055. I decide the hold knowingly, as the A350's final Do Nothing.

OVERRIDE CHECK
None is used. An override needs at least $1B over the best passing option. The Re-engine is +0.57 at best and trails by $0.42B in the worst column, and the Board would veto a Re-engine reached by override. My one override per game ends the game unused.

WHAT I ACCEPT, KNOWINGLY
I forgo about $0.57B in S1 ($0.47B weighted), for good. That is inside the band, so it is not a doctrine premium. The A350 stays at 70 a year and 41.2% share on the grid, competing on product and price, as older widebodies have before [A-0090, A-0091]. Its single engine source (Trent XWB) becomes a standing watch.

BOARD-GATE LINES
- Package: no Board item. Every field is at its default.
- For the record, the Re-engine not submitted:
  - Pillars: pass only if its EIS moves; a 2055-dated case would breach them.
  - Toepfer: fail on the added-move test (binding soft veto); cash passes.
  - Wagner: fail on engine readiness (binding soft veto); safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch pass.
  - Grid item: +0.57 x5 / -0.42 x2.
  - Not taken to the Board, since the Board's first condition (both pass, no override) is not met.

REACTION DISCIPLINE (rules 2 and 7)
- An fps launched now enters service in 2057 or later and needs no reply.
- NGSA is never cancelled.
- No Re-engine is approved, so a same-round 787 Re-engine triggers nothing.

DELAY TACTICS
Off for the whole game: none was ordered in any round from 2030 to 2050. The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) was never set aside, and I do not set it aside now. They are never named in public: the 2045 staffing clause is struck.

CONFIDENCE
My decision style is rated Low in the profile. Toepfer's and Wagner's tests are role-derived (Low and Very low).

frame.question:
What game are we playing, and how do we win? The same game as every round: the installed base, not share for its own sake. "We get paid in dollars, not in percentages."

This is the last decision year on the board, and the board leaves us one real choice. The Ducted, the Embraer partnership and the GEnx upgrade are all ready and counting, and each offers only hold. The only levers left are an Open Fan and lobbying on emissions. The airframer set that date a long time ago: the NGSA has been in service since 2037. An Open Fan launched today is ready in 2060, four years after the board's narrowbody window closes in 2056.

One thing is new, and I want it on the table rather than discovered later. The Open Fan's cost against hold is now $13.97B alone and $13.22B with Lobby. For the first time that is inside the $15B RISE allowance. That, plus "it's the last round", is exactly where my installed-base lens could talk us into a launch that buys nothing ("seeding the next 30 years"). So the question this round is not "can the allowance carry it?" It's "does an airframer want it inside the window?" On the record the answer is no.

So we win the last round the way we won the others:
1. The fleet flying today comes first: the LEAP fleet and our new single-aisle engine. The five field-data items we owe the Board stay open until the numbers exist. They don't close because the calendar runs out.
2. Keep delivering: kits and shop-visit material ahead of the OE delivery rate while OE volumes fall and the fleet ages.
3. Keep RISE whole as technology with Safran, and keep CFM on offer to every airframer.
4. Be candid. The round-3 forecast held to the cent. Both objectives end not met, and we gave up no PV for either.

Safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order, decide any tie.
