- S2's Boeing fps (2060 entry, code 7) is not on the record: Boeing said 'not this year' and gave no date. Even in S2 the item is -13.97.
- S2's 2060 entry falling in the same year an Open Fan would be ready is a coincidence, not a volume. The grid values neither.
Holding is not a cancel of RISE: RISE stays whole as technology (hard rule 5).

tests.name: Volumes first: Airbus supply answer and A320neo slots (ask 8)
tests.threshold: No number goes out before the airframer's volumes are agreed; I build an airframer's stated rate into the plan, not a figure of my own (inference: CX-0944 as a capital test, with CX-0981 and CX-0982)
tests.numbers:
Airbus's stated total is on the record, and it ties to the hold row. CFM's slice is not agreed, so it is a plan input and not a public number.
- Airbus's range is 2,612-2,732 NGSA engines a year across CFM and the Joint Venture (1,306-1,366 aircraft). 2,612 is exactly 2049's NGSA (1,306 aircraft x 2). Every year from 2046 to 2049 shows P&W equal to RR, so Airbus delivered no A320neo in those years (inference).
- The hold row implies 2,573-2,701 NGSA engines a year in 2050-56 (2,680 in 2050), and CFM's slice at 26.98% is 694-729 (723 in 2050). Your 705-737 is the same share applied to Airbus's range. Ties.
- The row sits at the low end of the range, a little below it in 2053-55. If Airbus ran at the top every year from 2050 to 2056, CFM would gain about +$0.21B of PV; at the floor, about -$0.07B (rough, inference). Neither is booked: guide low.
- My condition is met for planning to Airbus's stated rate. It is not met for a CFM number: the CFM allocation is worked inside the joint answer with Airbus and Safran, and no volume, rate or price goes out. Acknowledging the extension in public with no number is fine, Safran first.
- A320neo slots: on the observed data they are already back (28 A320neo in 2045, none from 2046), so there is no cost on the board. Off the board, flag LEAP-1A OE capacity that is no longer called, a risk of under-absorbing it. But the good news is that freed capacity can go to shop-visit material for an ageing fleet, where fewer OE engines help near-term profit. Don't add OE capacity to chase the top of Airbus's range: the range is below the 2,770 of 2044. Supply load is Ali's ground.
- LEAP kits: taken up. Record the line as CFM practice with Safran, at standard terms with no free upgrade.

tests.name: Volumes first: Embraer (ask 6)
tests.threshold: Embraer's value stays out of expected_pv_b until an Embraer volume is agreed; any real spend comes to my capex test and the Board first (inference: CX-0944)
tests.numbers:
- No Embraer airframe, volume or spend is agreed. The bulletin shows the partnership ready since 2042, and no Embraer airframe among the new narrowbodies.
- Its value inside the row, re-tied: +2.11 (model +2.108). That is 3.65 effective pp on the NGSA (28.33/105 = 26.98% against 23.33% without it), from 2042 to 2056, unchanged from round 3.
- It stays out of expected_pv_b: S1 -28.04 less 2.11 is -30.15.

tests.name: No overcapitalization, payout and rating (ask 7)
tests.threshold: New R&D and strain committed this round, spread over development years, at or below about $2.5B a year: what is left after returning more than 70% of about $8.5B of 2028 free cash flow (inference: an analogy from capex at 2-3% of revenue)
tests.numbers:
- Hold: $0 a year of new R&D or strain against about $2.55B of room (30% of $8.5B).
- The 70% payout ($5.95B) is whole.
- Rating: debt of $35B against EV of $160B (21.9%), with no new debt or commitment. No rating risk.
- For the record:
  - Open Fan: $0.8B a year ($8B over 10 years).
  - Open Fan + Lobby: $0.9B a year on my reading, $1.1B on the Board's. Even if Lobby's $1B falls in year one, the peak is $1.8B ($2.0B with strain), still inside the room.
  - They fail on pays-for-itself and the airframer path, not on the floor.
- Candidly, the hold row's -28.04 (17.5% of EV) is engine value below the status quo, not a balance-sheet charge. Lifecycle value is $22.2B against $31.7B in 2050 and $20.9B against $34.2B in 2056 (nominal). The payout stays at 70% of a smaller base.

tests.name: Premium in dollars
tests.threshold: Doctrine plus objective premium at most $2.0B a round and $4.0B a game. One RISE allowance up to $15B, declared in full against the best non-RISE plan (company doctrine; inference)
tests.numbers:
- Hold is the best plan in S1 and S2, so the premium is $0.
- Game total: $0 of $4.0B.
- The RISE allowance is unused, and it lapses unused at the end of the game, which is not a loss. $13.97B and $13.22B would fit inside $15B, but declaring it needs an airframer path (doctrine G1/G3) and an airframer volume (my rule), and neither is on the record. Nothing it would buy counts inside the window.
- No objective premium: neither objective can be bought on this grid.

tests.name: Column weights (ask 4)
tests.threshold: Weights rest on the record, not on early signals; a rival's standing public commitment is a live column (inference: CX-0896)
tests.numbers:
I accept .75 / .25 and don't challenge it.
- Boeing has no standing commitment on the record ('not launching a new airplane this year', no date). Its 'closer than it was' remark is an early signal, not a commitment.
- Every row is identical across the columns: hold -28.04, Open Fan item -13.97, Open Fan + Lobby item -13.22 on any mix. Nothing turns on the weights.
- Keeping .75 / .25 keeps the booking rule consistent with round 3.

tests.name: Reconciliation (ask 5)
tests.threshold: Tie round 3's forecast and book to today's row in numbers, and name each gap
tests.numbers:
- Round 3 forecast S1 -28.04, S2 -27.95, weighted -28.02. Boeing held, so S1 happened, and today's row is -28.04 to the cent. The -0.02 against the weighted figure is the S2 weight not realised.
- Round 3's year table matches today's line for line: 2045-49 shares 52.2 / 51.8 / 51.7 / 48.8 / 46.7%, engines 2,106 / 2,083 / 2,089 / 1,772 / 1,671, and the 2050-56 path (1,749 to 1,360).
- 2 x aircraft x share gives 2,106 / 2,082 / 2,090 / 1,770 / 1,671, within 2 engines each year.
- Book -30.15 against row -28.04: the $2.11B gap is Embraer's in-row value, held out until a volume is agreed. That is the rule working, not a forecast error.

tests.name: What the case leaves out (ask 10)
tests.threshold: Name the worst column for the recommended plan, its gap to the expected column, and the scenarios the expected case ignores
tests.numbers:
Worst column for hold: S1 = S2 = -28.04, a gap of $0.00 to the expected column.
Not in either column (rough, inference):
(a) Further MAX decline. The MAX is our sole-source slot. On the hold row it falls from about 513 aircraft (2050) to about 327 (2056). Its LEAP-1B engines for 2050-56 are worth about $6.98B of PV, so 10% fewer MAX is about -0.70.
(b) Airframer delivery slowdowns. CFM NB engines for 2050-56 are worth $12.94B of PV, so 5% fewer deliveries is about -0.65 and 10% about -1.29.
(c) Tariff escalation and a global recession: not in the grid.
(d) A widebody Re-engine or Trent 1000 upgrade undoing the GEnx step from 2053 (about 9 engines a year to 2061): about -0.23. None is on the record.
(e) Durability: the brief has no time-on-wing, inspection or kit data. Any reserve is booked in the round the need is found, not in this grid.
(f) Closed this round: any fps launched in 2050 enters service in 2057 at the earliest, after the 2056 window. Round 3's 7-year fps risk (about -2.4) no longer applies.

tests.name: Dated profit sequence
tests.threshold: For each launch: bill year, ready year and first year of share gain, inside the NB horizon to 2056 (inference: my dated sequences applied to the board)
tests.numbers:
Hold launches nothing.
- For the record, an Open Fan's sequence fails: bill from 2050 ($0.8B a year), ready in 2060 (Ali's date), no share gain inside the NB horizon, and a loss of all 26.98 NGSA points from 2050 to 2056.
- Programmes already running: Ducted ready 2041 (13.5% to 23.2% on the NGSA); Embraer counting 2042; GEnx counting 2042 (WB 42.0% to 44.8%). All are delivered.

tests.name: No second stack of projects (advice)
tests.threshold: Flag a plan with two or more projects (the $2B strain); each item passes only net of the strain it adds
tests.numbers:
- Hold runs no project in development. The Ducted, Embraer and GEnx are all ready, and the row's -2.00 of strain is sunk.
- An Open Fan, alone or with Lobby, carries no new strain on the grid.
- The GE9X is not live.

tests.name: Terms (ask 8, draft line)
tests.threshold: No launch-era pricing, no price concession, and no CFM narrowbody price, rate, capacity or volume talk without Safran, in any public statement or other move
tests.numbers:
Your draft line carries no price, concession, launch-era terms, volume, rate or delivery year.
- 'Airbus asked for long-term engine supply ... jointly with Safran' passes. To acknowledge the extension, use something like 'Airbus is extending its long-term engine supply agreements, and we're working that through with them, jointly with Safran', with Safran agreeing the wording first.
- Don't repeat Airbus's 2,612-2,732, any CFM slice, or the A320neo slots coming back: those are Airbus's numbers to give, or ours with Safran.
- 'Shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits stay ahead of the OE delivery rate' passes as CFM practice with Safran, at standard terms.
- The GEnx line is GE alone, won on product, with no price.
- 'On offer to every airframer' is an offer of supply, not of terms.

tests.name: Guide low (ask 9; advice)
tests.threshold: Recommend the low end of the expected column, with no upside before it is confirmed (inference: my guidance habit)
tests.numbers:
- Book expected_pv_b at -30.15: S1 hold (-28.04) less Embraer's +2.11 until a volume is agreed, the same rule as round 3.
- No upside is booked: no S2 difference exists, and the top of Airbus's range (+0.21) is not confirmed.
- I raise the guide to -28.04 when an Embraer volume is agreed.

vetoes.plan: Conditional: open_fan: launch, alone or with lobby_emissions: launch
vetoes.ground:
capex. My veto right is an inference from my price/cost and volumes-first record; under the team rule it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence.
- It fails pays-for-itself: the Open Fan alone is -13.97 in S1 and S2, $5.97B beyond its $8B bill, and Open Fan + Lobby is -13.22, $4.22B beyond $9B.
- It fails volumes-first: no airframer selection or volume exists for an Open Fan. The NGSA has been in service since 2037, and the Open Fan would be ready in 2060, after the 2056 window.
- My rule's one answer is a premium declared within the cap. In dollars the RISE allowance would hold it ($13.97B / $13.22B against $15B). But the doctrine's gates for that allowance (G1 committed airframer, G3 airframer free to take it inside the window, G4 test results) fail, so it cannot validly be declared.
This is not a cancel: RISE stays whole as technology (hard rule 5).

vetoes.plan: Conditional: lobby_emissions: launch without an Open Fan launched or live
vetoes.ground: capex: it fails pays-for-itself. My veto right is an inference that binds under the team rule unless answered with evidence. Lobby alone is about -1.00 in both columns (inference: a $1B bill and no grid row, with no effect without an Open Fan). With an Open Fan, it falls with the vetoed Open Fan.

vetoes.plan: Standing: any real Embraer spend, or any Embraer number, committed before an Embraer volume is agreed
vetoes.ground: capex: it fails volumes-first. My veto right is an inference from 'we need to work the exact volume assumptions', applied as a capital test; it binds under the team rule unless answered with evidence. No Embraer airframe, volume or spend is on the record, and none is proposed. Not triggered by Culp's lean.

vetoes.plan: Standing: any public statement or other move that offers launch-era pricing or a price concession, or gives CFM narrowbody price, rate, capacity or volume without Safran. That includes repeating Airbus's 2,612-2,732 range, a CFM slice of it, or the A320neo slots coming back
vetoes.ground: terms. My veto right is an inference from my pricing record and the joint-decision rule; it binds under the team rule, and on a statement alone the Board reads it as a recommendation. Culp's draft line and other moves pass as written. Acknowledging the Airbus extension with no number passes, Safran first.

vetoes.plan: Advice: expected_pv_b, weights, strain bills and reserves in the record
vetoes.ground:
Not a veto (advice only).
- Book -30.15, not -28.04: Embraer's +2.11 stays out until a volume is agreed.
- Keep .75 / .25 (nothing turns on it).
- State the Open Fan bills as $8B and $9B: the rows tie with no new strain (inference). The Board's $11B changes no call.
- Book any durability reserve in the round the need is found.
- Don't add LEAP OE capacity to chase the top of Airbus's range.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Six things would move me.
(1) An airframer puts on the record a new narrowbody entry that an Open Fan can meet, with a volume, jointly with Safran: then I test the RISE allowance in that round. No such entry fits inside this board's window.
(2) An Embraer volume is agreed: I raise the guide by about $2.1B, to -28.04.
(3) Airbus and Safran confirm CFM's slice at the top of the range: I raise the guide by up to about $0.2B once it is confirmed, not before.
(4) Ali brings a durability or safety flag on field data: the holds don't change, but I book the reserve in the round we find it, and the agenda changes.
(5) Safran declines the joint Airbus wording, or wants terms in public: I re-run the terms test.
(6) The GM's strain rule differs from my reading: I restate the bills. No call turns on it.
cfo.memo:
Larry, the books tie.

Your items match to the cent, identical in both columns: Open Fan -13.97, with Lobby -13.22, Lobby on top +0.75. My model gets -13.96, -13.21 and +0.75 with no new strain: 26.98 points of NGSA share at $0.221B a point is $5.96B, plus $8B; 19.05 points is $4.21B, plus $9B. So the bills are $8B and $9B (inference).

Be clear on why the cost fell from $20B to $14B: the window got shorter, not the case better. The allowance now holds the dollars, but no airframer volume stands behind it and nothing counts after 2056. It's a ceiling, not a budget. No financial case uses it. Premium $0; game total $0 of $4.0B.

Reconciliation: round 3's S1 -28.04 held to the cent, and the 2045-56 year table is unchanged. Book -30.15 against the row's -28.04: the $2.11B is Embraer, held out by rule. No Embraer airframe, volume or spend is agreed.

Floor: no new R&D or strain, the $5.95B payout whole, $35B of debt on $160B of EV, no rating risk.

Airbus's range ties: 2,612 is exactly 2049's NGSA engines; the row runs 2,573-2,701 through 2056, our slice 694-729. We don't book the top (+$0.2B). Acknowledge the extension with no number, Safran first.

Left out: 10% fewer MAX is -0.70, 5% fewer deliveries -0.65, plus tariffs, recession and any durability reserve, booked when found.

But the good news is the base is paying, and there's nothing to hide.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (my date veto): every ready year in the orders and options (Culp's ask 4)
tests.threshold: No ready year earlier than the board's development time: Ducted at launch + 6; Open Fan at launch + 10 and not before 2045; Embraer counts at launch + 7; GEnx at launch + 3 and not before 2035. An order whose value depends on an earlier year fails. Inference: my test standard applied to the board's development times.
tests.numbers:
Recomputed from rules.md (Ducted ready 6 years after launch; Open Fan 10 years after launch and not before 2045) and the brief.
- Ducted (hold only): 2035 + 6 = 2041. Ready since 2041.
- Embraer (hold only): 2035 + 7 = 2042. Counting since 2042.
- GEnx (hold only): 2030 + 3 = 2033. Its value counts from 2042 (WB share 44.8%), which is after 2035.
- Open Fan (options B and C): max(2050 + 10, 2045) = 2060.

Grid (S1 rivals hold / S2 Boeing 10-year fps, code 7):
- hold: -28.04 / -28.04;
- Open Fan: -42.01 / -42.01;
- Open Fan + Lobby: -41.26 / -41.26.
Items against hold, which I recomputed to the cent:
- Open Fan: -13.97;
- Open Fan + Lobby: -13.22;
- Lobby on top of the Open Fan: +0.75.
All are identical in both columns.

Both Open Fan rows carry the wait penalty, so they are valued on 2060, not on an earlier year. Hold adds no date. No option's value rests on a year earlier than the board allows.

Objective: 'launched and ready by 2050' cannot be met, because 2050 + 10 = 2060. Any premium or claim resting on it would rest on a year ten years early, and it would fail my test. Culp claims none.

What test stands behind 2041? None on ducted hardware in my evidence. It is the board's development time, now on the public record. I report no slip and certify no gate result, because I have evidence of neither.

tests.name: Test, not analysis (my date veto): Culp's draft public line and other moves (Culp's ask 7)
tests.threshold: Every date in the public statement or other moves must be one a test can back. No Open Fan or RISE entry before 2045, no ready year before launch plus development years, and no RISE ground-test, flight-test or entry year (hard rule 6).
tests.numbers:
Line by line, the draft has no year anywhere.
- 'Safety, quality, delivery and cost': no date.
- 'the LEAP fleet and our new single-aisle engine flying with our customers': still stands on the record. The Ducted has been ready since 2041, the NGSA has been in service since 2037, and Airbus says in public that the NGSA 'flies on ... engine supply from CFM'. That it is our Ducted flying is my reading (inference); the table says 'ready'. Add nothing to it: no cycles, no time on wing, no 'durable', 'mature' or 'proven', and no year. 'New' after nine years is a name, not a claim.
- 'We'll keep telling you what we're seeing in the field': no date, but see the wording advice. We have told the Board deliveries only, and published no durability field data.
- 'kits stay ahead of the OE delivery rate': no date. It is our priority rule, not a measured result: there is no kit data. Attach no number.
- Airbus answer 'jointly with Safran': no rate, no year and no slot count. Airbus's 2,612-2,732 range stays out.
- 'RISE ... the airframers will set its date': no ground-test, flight-test or entry year. My 2022 'middle of this decade' fly demo became 'this decade'. Promise none.
- No 'next generation', no Ducted figure, no rival named.
- The 'after October 2025' sentence moves to private. I agree: it tells the market how old our last RISE result is.

Other moves (i) to (vii) carry no public year. 2060, 2056 and 2037 stay in the rationale and with the Board.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Open Fan (advice; Culp's ask 4)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. An Open Fan ready no later than the first new narrowbody's entry into service avoids the 35 pp wait penalty (20 pp with Lobby). Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers:
The first new narrowbody is the NGSA, in service since 2037.
- Launch 2050, ready 2060: 23 years after the NGSA, and 4 years after the board's NB window closes in 2056.
- S2: a 10-year fps launched in 2050 enters service in 2060, the same year. But rules.md triggers the penalty on the FIRST new narrowbody, and the NGSA came first. So the penalty applies in both columns, and the identical rows confirm it: Open Fan -13.97 and Open Fan + Lobby -13.22 in S1 and S2.
- S2's 2060 is not an airframer path. It is the board's column, not a Boeing date: Boeing said 'I'm not going to give you a date'. The board counts NB only to 2056, so nothing after the window is valued.
- The $15B allowance covers $13.22B to $13.97B, but money does not move a ready year.

2060 is the correct ready year, so this is not my veto. Hard rule 2 bars the launch.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted and Embraer (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap. A defensive Ducted ready after the airframe's entry still earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new narrowbody is in service, so lateness does not fail it. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers:
- Ducted: ready 2041, 4 years after the NGSA's 2037 entry. It has earned its +10 pp on the NGSA since 2041.
- Embraer: counts from 2042, 5 years after the NGSA.
- S2: a 2060 fps entry is 19 years after the Ducted's ready year, if Boeing keeps code 7.
All are hold only. There is nothing to launch.

tests.name: Physics (wording check)
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A ducted engine has 'less than half' the gain, so it is never the next generation. That it is a defensive step only is doctrine (hard rule 3), not my words. Without a fuel-burn claim this is a wording check on the statement (inference).
tests.numbers:
- Neither the brief nor the draft line makes a fuel-burn claim.
- 'Next generation' does not appear, and 'our new single-aisle engine' is not a next-generation claim.
- H3 holds: the Ducted gets 'less than half' the open fan's gain. It is a defence.
- Culp's 20% line binds RISE. No RISE product is proposed, so the line is not engaged, and there is nothing to strike or rebut.

RISE facts for the Board, to October 2025 only: designed for 'more than 20%' fuel burn, ready for sustainable aviation fuel and hydrogen-capable. In tests with Airbus, open-fan noise came in below the LEAP's.

tests.name: Durability first: no plan trades durability for fuel burn or schedule
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers:
- Hold everything trades nothing: no new programme, no fuel-burn target and no schedule to compress.
- The plan keeps kits and shop-visit material ahead of OE rate.
- The Open Fan options would start a new hot-section development on the constrained suppliers while the installed fleet's durability data is still open (see supply load).
- The draft drops round 3's 'we don't trade durability for fuel burn'. That is a commitment, not a figure, and it can stay or go. Culp's call.

tests.name: Open item (a), Culp's ask 2a: the Ducted's harsh and neutral cycles on the fleet leaders, and the gate's turn-on, turn-off results
tests.threshold: Harsh time on wing against the CFM56's 7,000-8,000 cycles, not the LEAP's about 4,800. Company target: 8,000 harsh and 17,000 neutral. The gate passes on turn-on, turn-off testing. Field or test data only.
tests.numbers:
OPEN. Not applicable because the test cannot be run. This is not a pass.
- The fleet has been in service nine years (2041-2050). The brief's only field data is deliveries: no time-on-wing, harsh-cycle or removal data.
- My evidence ends in 2025, before any ducted hardware existed.
- Did the gate pass before 2041? There is no evidence either way. The record shows 'ready 2041' on the board's development time.
- Nobody claims the yardstick is met, in public or in private, until the numbers exist.
- In 2035 we promised field numbers by 2045. Five years later we still don't have them. The item does not close because 2050 is the last decision year.

tests.name: Open item (b), Culp's ask 2b: enhanced-inspection findings on safety-critical parts, in new make and MRO
tests.threshold: Findings reported from the first engine on, in new-make shops and in MRO. Any finding on a safety-critical part is a flag, and it goes to the Board at once with a cross-functional answer.
tests.numbers: OPEN. Enhanced inspection is institutionalised in new-make shops and MRO (my 2024 words). The brief carries no inspection data, so I have no findings to report: none found, and none reported clean. No flag, because no finding.

tests.name: Open item (c), Culp's ask 2c: the LEAP-1B kit's certification outcome
tests.threshold: A durability fix counts only when it is certified and the failure is turned off in test. A kit that does not turn the harsh-environment failure off is an installed-fleet flag, ahead of any programme.

tests.name: Open item (d), Culp's ask 2d: clearance of the 9 suppliers at 15 sites
tests.threshold: Each of the 9 suppliers at 15 sites cleared on supplier-level field data: material in, on time, to quality. Inference: my supply role is in Culp's words only.
tests.numbers: OPEN. The brief has no supplier-level data. I do not certify them on analysis. Delivery-level data (item 3) shows no shortfall in OE engines. That is consistent with the suppliers carrying the load, but it is not a clearance. No evidence: following doctrine.

tests.name: Open item (e), Culp's ask 2e: kits and shop-visit material against the OE delivery rate
tests.threshold: Kits and shop-visit material ahead of the OE delivery rate, on field data. Any rationing call goes to a cross-functional team.
tests.numbers:
OPEN on the kit leg. The brief has no kit or shop-visit data.
- OE load is falling: CFM NB engines go from 2,106 (2045) to 1,749 (2050) and 1,360 (2056). That is 357 and 746 engines lower (-35.4% by 2056), and 1,244 (-47.8%) below the 2036 peak of 2,604. A320neo slots come back as the lines close.
- Does that free supplier capacity for shop-visit material? I can't say on field data. Lower OE load points that way, but an ageing fleet pulls more shop visits, and I have no hot-section supplier numbers to net the two. That would be analysis, and I will not certify it.
- The rule stands: kits first, and any rationing call goes to a cross-functional team.

tests.name: Delivery leg on field data (Culp's ask 3)
tests.threshold: Every year, CFM NB engines delivered = 2 x aircraft delivered x CFM share, to within share rounding. Nothing on the record shows an aircraft waiting on a CFM engine.

tests.name: Supply load (seat doctrine; Culp's ask 6)
tests.threshold: Two or more projects cost $2B of strain and load the same constrained suppliers. Recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain. Inference: my supply role is in Culp's words only (the board's strain rule).
tests.numbers:
Hold adds no project and no strain. R&D stays at -4.00 (the 2035 Ducted, sunk) and strain at -2.00 (sunk), both already in the row.

Confirmed, as doctrine and not my record:
- An Open Fan would put a new compact core and fan on the same constrained hot-section suppliers that carry LEAP kits, shop-visit material and Ducted production.
- Lobby loads no supplier.
- Whether the board books strain on Open Fan + Lobby (a $9B or $11B bill) is Ghai's to tie. On the shop floor there is one hardware project.

The grid doesn't pay for it: -13.97 alone and -13.22 with Lobby. I recommend against.

No evidence: following doctrine.

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign
tests.threshold: On the widebody, prefer the GEnx upgrade on a proven architecture to a new engine. On the narrowbody, keep RISE technology flowing into the in-service engines while RISE matures (inference).
tests.numbers:
- GEnx: hold only. Proven architecture, ready since 2033, counting since 2042 at 44.8% WB. Taking it to 787 customers puts the same proven engine on more aircraft.
- Narrowbody: RISE technology keeps flowing into the LEAP and the Ducted while RISE stays technology.

tests.name: Safety call and flag status (Culp's ask 1)
tests.threshold: Any problem or order that touches safety or durability goes to a cross-functional team, never to one person. Any flag goes to the Board at once, with the cross-functional answer on evidence.

tests.name: RISE test record and the doctrine's G4 gate (Culp's ask 5)
tests.threshold: No RISE product without test results turned on and turned off, including compact-core durability. No RISE date in public.
tests.numbers:
No Open Fan is proposed. My latest RISE items are dated 21 October 2025:
- compact-core HPT dust testing began that month, the earliest we have ever started it;
- the first Chief Mechanic and Architect for Open Fan durability was named.
Before that:
- open-fan noise came in below the LEAP's in tests with Airbus;
- ground and flight test were promised 'this decade', slipped from my 2022 'middle of this decade'.

No test result after October 2025 is in my evidence, including whether the flight test flew. So G4 is not met for a product, whatever the allowance says. RISE stays whole, with no ground-test, flight-test or entry year in public.

vetoes.plan:
CONDITIONAL, NOT TRIGGERED: no standing objection. Neither option A nor Culp's draft line trips it, so Culp has no failed test to answer. It applies only to:
(a) any Open Fan order, premium or claim valued on a ready year before 2060 (a 2050 launch). That includes any claim resting on the 'ready by 2050' objective.
(b) any public statement or other move that gives a Ducted, Embraer, Open Fan or RISE ready, entry, ground-test or flight-test year, or any other date no test backs. That includes presenting S2's 2060 fps entry as an airframer date for RISE.
vetoes.ground:
Dates not backed by real testing, binding grounds 1 and 2: 'if it's not turn on and turn off, I will not believe the outcomes'; 'it's not on the back of a theory. It's not on the back of analysis.'

Inference note: my words date from 2024, when I was VP of Engineering, and concern whether to believe durability-fix results. That they give me a veto over programme dates is an inference. Under the team rule it binds unless Culp answers it with test evidence.

Every value on the grid rests on the board's development times (2041, 2042, 2060), and the draft statement has no year, so nothing is vetoed now. I will re-check the final orders and statement at the veto check.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch in 2050, alone or with lobby_emissions: launch
vetoes.ground:
Advice, not a date veto: 2060 is the correct ready year.
- It is 23 years after the NGSA's 2037 entry and 4 years after the 2056 window, so the wait penalty applies in both columns: -13.97 alone, -13.22 with Lobby.
- S2's 2060 fps is not a path. The first new narrowbody came first, and Boeing has given no date.
- The $15B allowance covers the cost but does not move a ready year.
- No RISE test result after October 2025 is in my evidence, so no test backs a product (G4).
- It would stack a new hot section on the constrained suppliers that carry the installed fleet.
Hard rule 2 bars it. Keep RISE whole as technology. We failed twice. We got it done.

vetoes.plan: lobby_emissions: launch without an Open Fan
vetoes.ground: Advice. There is no date issue, because Lobby takes effect at once, but it does nothing on its own (about -1.00, inference; no row). No evidence: following Culp and doctrine. Technical facts, if ever needed: RISE is designed to be SAF-ready and hydrogen-capable, and open-fan noise came in below the LEAP's in tests with Airbus.

vetoes.plan: Wording in Culp's draft public statement
vetoes.ground:
Advice, not a date veto.
- 'We'll keep telling you what we're seeing in the field' implies a record of field reporting. We have reported deliveries only, never durability. Say 'We'll tell you what we're seeing in the field, and what we don't know yet', as in round 3. No deny-then-reverse later.
- Keep 'our new single-aisle engine flying with our customers' and add nothing to it: no cycles, time on wing, 'durable', 'mature' or 'proven'.
- 'Kits ... stay ahead of the OE delivery rate' is our priority rule. Attach no number; we have no kit data.
- Keep the 'after October 2025' RISE sentence private.
- No 2060, 2056 or 2037 in public. Never 'next generation' for the Ducted.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Only test or field data would change my mind, never analysis.
(1) A flag. A finding in the field or in inspection would be one: a harsh-environment failure turned on that the design does not turn off, a finding on a safety-critical part, or a Ducted or LEAP fleet leader removed short of the CFM56's 7,000-8,000 harsh cycles. I raise it at once, with the cross-functional answer. The holds stay; the agenda and the statement change.
(2) The LEAP-1B kit. A certification result showing the kit does not turn the harsh-environment failure off is an installed-fleet flag, ahead of everything.
(3) Supply. Field data showing kits or shop-visit material behind OE rate, OE deliveries below airframer rate, or a supplier site not cleared. Then kits come first, and the rationing call goes cross-functional.
(4) The Open Fan. Nothing on this board moves it. I would need an airframer on the record with a first-new-narrowbody entry no earlier than the Open Fan's ready year, plus RISE ground-test, flight-test and compact-core durability results turned on and turned off. With the NGSA flying since 2037 and the window closing in 2056, that cannot happen in this game.
ops.memo:
I report back against what we promised.

Flag status: no flag. A flag is a failure turned on in test or found in the field. I have none, and raise none on analysis. Missing data is not a pass.

The five items: all five open. The Ducted fleet leaders have nine years in service, and I cannot give you one harsh cycle against the CFM56's 7,000 to 8,000. Inspection findings: open. LEAP-1B kit: open; my last record says certification in early 2026. The 9 suppliers at 15 sites: open. Kits against OE rate: open. In 2035 we promised numbers by 2045. We missed it. Nothing closes because the calendar runs out.

Deliveries: 1,671 engines on 1,789 aircraft at 46.7% in 2049. Every year since 2045 ties within 2 engines. Nothing on the record shows an aircraft waiting on us.

Dates. Ducted 2041. Embraer 2042. GEnx 2033. An Open Fan launched today is ready in 2060: 23 years after the NGSA, 4 after the window. The allowance pays for a programme; it does not move a ready year. S2's 2060 is not a path: the first new narrowbody came first. No RISE result after October 2025 is in my evidence. My date test passes. No veto.

Supply: hold adds none. An Open Fan puts a new core on the suppliers carrying LEAP kits.

Wording: "keep telling you" claims a field record we never published. Say "tell you".

Hold everything. RISE whole. We failed twice. We got it done.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Our first job is still the fleet flying today: the LEAP fleet and our new single-aisle engine, flying with our customers. We'll tell you what we're seeing in the field, and we'll tell you what we don't know yet. Shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits stay ahead of the OE delivery rate as the fleet ages, and we don't trade durability for fuel burn.

Airbus is extending its long-term engine supply agreements, and we're working that through with them, jointly with Safran. CFM's engines stay on offer to every airframer. We don't have a birthright on anybody's next order. We have to earn it, one engine at a time.

On the 787, we'll keep making the GEnx better for Boeing's customers.

RISE stays a technology programme we're all in on with Safran, and the airframers will set its date.

No new programme this round. We're running the business we've got, and running it well. It's that simple. Ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: hold everything (Do Nothing) on every field. Every order is at default, so there is no Board item.
- Hold is the best plan in both columns: -28.04 in S1 and S2 (yield 82.47%).
- Premium $0. The game total ends at $0 of $4.0B, and the RISE allowance goes unused.
- No overrides.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
It's the installed base, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0630, CX-0493].
This is the last decision year on the board. The Ducted, the Embraer partnership and the GEnx upgrade are all ready and counting, and each offers only hold. The live levers are open_fan and lobby_emissions, and the airframer set that date long ago: the NGSA has been in service since 2037.
We win the last round the way we won the others: the fleet first, delivery, RISE kept whole, CFM on offer to every airframer, and candour about what we know and what we don't.

GRID (S1 rivals hold / S2 Boeing 10-year fps, code 7)
- Rows: hold -28.04 / -28.04; Open Fan -42.01 / -42.01; Open Fan + Lobby -41.26 / -41.26.
- Items against hold, verified to the cent by both Ghai and Ali:
  - Open Fan alone -13.97;
  - Open Fan item with Lobby also at default -13.22;
  - Lobby on top of the Open Fan +0.75;
  - Lobby alone about -1.00 (inference; no row).
- Every row is identical across the columns, so on any mix of weights hold is -28.04 and the Open Fan item -13.97. S2 changes nothing: an fps launched in 2050 on a 10-year clock enters service in 2060, after the narrowbody window closes in 2056. Even a 7-year clock (2057) would miss it.

MY TESTS
1. What game, and no birthright [CX-0564, CX-0587]: no column has a rival taking a CFM slot inside the window. In S2, Boeing selects all three makers, but only from 2060. Off the grid an airframer can change its code before entry into service, which is why CFM stays on offer to everyone (H1).
2. Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0609]: no launch beats hold.
   - A new narrowbody has been on the record since 2037, so S1 shows the launch's own effect: -13.97 alone, $5.97B beyond its $8B bill, and -13.22 with Lobby, $4.22B beyond $9B.
   - The excess is the wait penalty: CFM's 26.98 pp on the NGSA goes to zero from 2050 to 2056 (19.05 pp lost with Lobby), at about $0.221B per pp (Ghai's model; inference).
   - It buys no share inside the window, no objective, and nothing the board counts after 2056. Nothing makes that risk worth taking.
3. Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]: S1. Boeing said it is "not launching a new airplane this year" and gave no date.
4. The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469].
   - An Open Fan launched in 2050 is ready in 2060 (Ali): 23 years after the NGSA's entry and 4 years after the window closes.
   - The one exception is the RISE allowance, for a launch I judge strategic. For the first time the dollars fit: $13.97B alone and $13.22B with Lobby, against $15B. That's because the window got shorter (7 years of penalty instead of 12), not because the case got better (Ghai).
   - I don't judge it strategic. The doctrine's gates in front of the allowance fail: G1 (a committed airframer), G3 (an airframer free to take it inside the window) and G4 (RISE test results after October 2025; Ali has none). Only G5, the dollars, passes.
   - S2's fps entering in 2060, the same year an Open Fan would be ready, is a coincidence, not a path. The first new narrowbody came first, Boeing has given no date, and the grid values nothing after 2056.
   - The allowance is a ceiling, not a budget. It lapses unused, and that is not a loss.
   - I'm naming my own bias so we don't act on it: the installed-base lens ("seeding the next 20, the next 30 years" [CX-0555], "the price of admission" [CX-0557]) plus "it's the last round, use it or lose it". "It's really not for us to say when we're going to see that architecture EIS" [CX-0205]. No airframer has asked for it.
5. Ducted only as a defence (H3): it has been ready since 2041 and has earned its +10 pp on the NGSA since then. There is nothing to decide, and it is never called the next generation.
6. Can the suppliers carry it [CX-0613, CX-0633]: hold adds no project and no strain. An Open Fan would put a new compact core and fan on the same hot-section suppliers that carry LEAP kits and shop material (Ali; doctrine).
7. The next generation [CX-0217, CX-0208]: no fuel-burn claim, and no "next generation" wording. The 20% line binds RISE; no RISE product is proposed, so it isn't engaged, and there is nothing to strike or rebut.
8. Tie-break: not needed. Hold leads the next-best row by $13.22B, far outside the $1B ε.
9. Premium cap (H9): $0 this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game.

EXCO, UNDER THE TEAM RULE
I proposed hold, and both colleagues recommend hold on every field.
- Ghai's binding vetoes are all conditional or standing, and none is triggered:
  - an Open Fan, alone or with Lobby;
  - Lobby alone;
  - Embraer spend or numbers before a volume is agreed;
  - price, rate, capacity or volume talk without Safran, which includes repeating Airbus's range, a CFM slice of it, or the A320neo slots coming back.
  The statement passes his terms test, and I used his wording for the Airbus extension.
- Ali's date veto is conditional and not triggered: every value rests on the board's development times (2041, 2042, 2060), and no public line or public move carries a year.
- Ali raises no safety or durability flag.
- So I have no failed test to answer, and overrides is empty.

STRAIN READING (re-tied, inference)
- Ghai's model ties the rows with no new strain: $5.96B plus $8B gives -13.96, and $4.21B plus $9B gives -13.21, against the grid's -13.97 and -13.22.
- With $2B of strain the rows would read -15.97 and -15.22, and neither ties. So the bills are $8B and $9B.
- The Board's $11B reading changes no call.
- Ali: on the shop floor there is one hardware project, and Lobby loads no supplier.

SAFRAN GATE (H7) [CX-0184, CX-0166]
- open_fan (hold): RISE stays the 50-50 technology programme. We ask Safran to fund no product that no airframer can take inside the window, and holding asks nothing of the partner.
- lobby_emissions (hold): it serves RISE and is not proposed without an Open Fan, so nothing goes to Safran.
- ducted (hold): it is ready, a defence of the installed base both partners share. No new order.
- partner_embraer (hold): no new order. Anything that goes to Embraer goes to Safran first.
- The Airbus long-term supply answer stays joint, with price, rate and capacity to Safran first. Safran agrees the public acknowledgement's wording first.
- LEAP kits and shop-visit material are CFM practice with Safran.
- genx: GE alone, no gate.

RECONCILIATION (candid, in numbers)
- Round 3 forecast S1 -28.04, S2 -27.95, weighted -28.02. Boeing held, so S1 happened, and today's row is -28.04: it held to the cent. The -0.02 against the weighted figure is the S2 weight that didn't happen.
- Round 3's year table matches line for line:
  - shares in 2045-49: 52.2 / 51.8 / 51.7 / 48.8 / 46.7%;
  - engines in 2045-49: 2,106 / 2,083 / 2,089 / 1,772 / 1,671;
  - the 2050-56 path (1,749 down to 1,360) is unchanged.
- Delivery leg: 2 x aircraft x share ties to the delivered engines within 1.5 engines every year (Ali).
- Book against row: -30.15 against -28.04. The $2.11B gap is Embraer's in-row value, held out by rule until a volume is agreed. That is the rule working, not a forecast error.
- What moved in S2: last round S2 was +0.09 better for hold (an fps entering in 2055). Now that entry would be 2060, so the difference is gone.

AIRBUS EXTENSION (Ghai's volumes-first test)
- Airbus's public range ties to the hold row:
  - 2,612 is exactly 2049's NGSA engines;
  - the row implies 2,573-2,701 a year in 2050-56, with a CFM slice of 694-729 (723 in 2050).
- The top of the range would be worth about +$0.21B and the floor about -$0.07B. Neither is booked.
- The condition is met for planning to Airbus's stated rate. It is not met for a CFM number.
- We acknowledge the extension in public with no number, Safran first.

WHAT WE KNOW AND WHAT WE DON'T
- What we know: deliveries. Every year from 2045 to 2049 ties, and nothing on the record shows an aircraft waiting on a CFM engine.
- The drop below 50% comes mainly from the MAX, our sole-source slot: Boeing deliveries fell from 684 to 483. Ali reads that as the demand side, since Boeing's waiting backlog runs to zero (inference). We keep that private and make no comment on Boeing.
- What we don't know: all five field-data items are open. In 2035 we told the Board it would have numbers by 2045, and in 2050 we still don't. That's a miss, and I own it. None of this changes a hold. Nothing closes because the calendar runs out.

WHAT THE CASE LEAVES OUT (Ghai's rough figures; inference)
- Further MAX decline: 10% fewer is about -0.70.
- Airframer delivery slowdowns: 5% fewer is about -0.65, 10% about -1.29.
- A widebody Re-engine undoing the GEnx step: about -0.23.
- Tariffs and recession.
- Any durability reserve, booked when the need is found.
- Worst column for hold: S1 = S2, a $0 gap.

FLOOR (Ghai)
- No new R&D or strain against about $2.55B of room.
- The 70% payout ($5.95B on about $8.5B) is whole.
- Debt of $35B against EV of $160B: no rating risk.
- Candidly, -28.04 is engine value below the status quo, not a balance-sheet charge. The payout stays at 70% of a smaller base.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD
My record doesn't address Embraer handling, Lobby, the game's Open Fan window or the use of the RISE allowance and its G1-G5 gates. Company doctrine (profile section 6; dashboard_game sections 2 and 5) drove those calls. Money follows Ghai's tests; dates and readiness follow Ali's.

AFTER THE BOARD
This was the last decision year, and the holds stand. Four items carry forward as standing items: the five field-data items, the Embraer condition, the joint Airbus answer, and RISE whole as technology. If an airframer puts on the record an entry an Open Fan can meet, that is the path RISE was built for. It comes to the Board jointly with Safran.

memo_weighing.ops:
Ali's record is thin: his own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering. On supply, his record is only my description of his job [CX-0633], so I checked those parts against doctrine.
- Date test: passes. Every value rests on the board's development times (2041, 2042, 2060), and no public line or move carries a year. His conditional veto binds nothing here.
- Open Fan: his advice matches hard rule 2 and the grid. 2060 is the right ready year, S2's 2060 is not a path, and the allowance pays for a programme but does not move a ready year.
- Flags: I took his flag status exactly. There is no flag, because a flag is a finding, but missing data is not a pass. All five items are reported as OPEN.
- G4: his RISE evidence ends in October 2025, so G4 is not met for a product.
- Supply: his view (an Open Fan stacks a new core on the constrained hot-section suppliers; Lobby loads none) is consistent with the board's strain rule and with Ghai's tie, so I accept it. His refusal to net lower OE load against more shop visits without supplier data is right, and the call goes to the cross-functional team.
- Wording: adopted. 'tell you', not 'keep telling you'. 'Our new single-aisle engine, flying with our customers' is kept with nothing added. No year, no Ducted figure, no 'next generation'. The 'after October 2025' sentence moves to private.
- I kept 'we don't trade durability for fuel burn' in the statement, which he left to me: it is a commitment, not a figure [CX-0208].
No binding ground of his is engaged.

decision.premium_reason:
$0. The submitted plan (hold everything) is the best grid plan in both columns, so nothing is given up.
- Doctrine or objective premium: $0 this round. The game total ends at $0 of $4.0B.
- RISE allowance: not used, and stated apart.
  - For the first time the dollars would fit: the Open Fan costs $13.97B alone and $13.22B with Lobby against the best non-RISE plan (hold), inside $15B. That is because the window got shorter, not because the case got better.
  - The allowance needs an airframer path, and there is none in any column. The NGSA has been the first new narrowbody since 2037, and a 2050 launch is ready in 2060, after the 2056 window, so the wait penalty applies everywhere.
  - The doctrine's gates G1 (a committed airframer), G3 (an airframer free to take it inside the window) and G4 (RISE test results after October 2025) fail; only G5, the dollars, passes.
  - S2's 2060 fps entry is a coincidence, not a path.
  - The allowance lapses unused at the end of the game, and that is not a loss.
- No objective premium could buy anything: NB share can't be lifted by any lever, and no Open Fan can be ready by 2050.
decision.objective_note:
The mission never changes the payoff, and no PV is given up for it.
- Dominate NB (at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050): 68.3%, 52.2% and 47.2% on hold. Not met, because of 2050. No grid lever lifts it:
  - the Ducted and Embraer are already counting;
  - an Open Fan only takes share away (35 pp, or 20 pp with Lobby);
  - Lobby alone does nothing.
  The drop below 50% comes mainly from fewer MAX deliveries, our sole-source slot, which is not a lever we hold.
- Introduce the Open Fan (launched and ready by 2050): not met and out of reach. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060, launch + 10.
- Both end not met, with no PV given up for either. I report this to the Board in private, not in public.

final.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Our first job is still the fleet flying today: the LEAP fleet and our new single-aisle engine, flying with our customers. We'll tell you what we're seeing in the field, and we'll tell you what we don't know yet. Shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits stay ahead of the OE delivery rate as the fleet ages, and we don't trade durability for fuel burn.

Airbus is extending its long-term engine supply agreements, and we're working that through with them, jointly with Safran. CFM's engines stay on offer to every airframer. We don't have a birthright on anybody's next order. We have to earn it, one engine at a time.

On the 787, we'll keep making the GEnx better for Boeing's customers.

RISE stays a technology programme we're all in on with Safran, and the airframers will set its date.

No new programme this round. We're running the business we've got, and running it well. It's that simple. Ain't that hard.
final.rationale:
DECISION: hold everything (Do Nothing) on every field. Every order is at default, so there is no Board item.
- Hold is the best plan in both columns: -28.04 in S1 and S2 (yield 82.47%).
- Premium $0. The game total ends at $0 of $4.0B, and the RISE allowance goes unused.
- No overrides.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
It's the installed base, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0630, CX-0493].
This is the last decision year on the board. The Ducted, the Embraer partnership and the GEnx upgrade are all ready and counting, and each offers only hold. The live levers are open_fan and lobby_emissions, and the airframer set that date long ago: the NGSA has been in service since 2037.
We win the last round the way we won the others: the fleet first, delivery, RISE kept whole, CFM on offer to every airframer, and candour about what we know and what we don't.

GRID (S1 rivals hold / S2 Boeing 10-year fps, code 7)
- Rows: hold -28.04 / -28.04; Open Fan -42.01 / -42.01; Open Fan + Lobby -41.26 / -41.26.
- Items against hold, verified to the cent by both Ghai and Ali:
  - Open Fan alone -13.97;
  - Open Fan item with Lobby also at default -13.22;
  - Lobby on top of the Open Fan +0.75;
  - Lobby alone about -1.00 (inference; no row).
- Every row is identical across the columns, so on any mix of weights hold is -28.04 and the Open Fan item -13.97. S2 changes nothing: an fps launched in 2050 on a 10-year clock enters service in 2060, after the narrowbody window closes in 2056. Even a 7-year clock (2057) would miss it.

MY TESTS
1. What game, and no birthright [CX-0564, CX-0587]: no column has a rival taking a CFM slot inside the window. In S2, Boeing selects all three makers, but only from 2060. Off the grid an airframer can change its code before entry into service, which is why CFM stays on offer to everyone (H1).
2. Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0609]: no launch beats hold.
   - A new narrowbody has been on the record since 2037, so S1 shows the launch's own effect: -13.97 alone, $5.97B beyond its $8B bill, and -13.22 with Lobby, $4.22B beyond $9B.
   - The excess is the wait penalty: CFM's 26.98 pp on the NGSA goes to zero from 2050 to 2056 (19.05 pp lost with Lobby), at about $0.221B per pp (Ghai's model; inference).
   - It buys no share inside the window, no objective, and nothing the board counts after 2056. Nothing makes that risk worth taking.
3. Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]: S1. Boeing said it is "not launching a new airplane this year" and gave no date.
4. The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469].
   - An Open Fan launched in 2050 is ready in 2060 (Ali): 23 years after the NGSA's entry and 4 years after the window closes.
   - The one exception is the RISE allowance, for a launch I judge strategic. For the first time the dollars fit: $13.97B alone and $13.22B with Lobby, against $15B. That's because the window got shorter (7 years of penalty instead of 12), not because the case got better (Ghai).
   - I don't judge it strategic. The doctrine's gates in front of the allowance fail: G1 (a committed airframer), G3 (an airframer free to take it inside the window) and G4 (RISE test results after October 2025; Ali has none). Only G5, the dollars, passes.
   - S2's fps entering in 2060, the same year an Open Fan would be ready, is a coincidence, not a path. The first new narrowbody came first, Boeing has given no date, and the grid values nothing after 2056.
   - The allowance is a ceiling, not a budget. It lapses unused, and that is not a loss.
   - I'm naming my own bias so we don't act on it: the installed-base lens ("seeding the next 20, the next 30 years" [CX-0555], "the price of admission" [CX-0557]) plus "it's the last round, use it or lose it". "It's really not for us to say when we're going to see that architecture EIS" [CX-0205]. No airframer has asked for it.
5. Ducted only as a defence (H3): it has been ready since 2041 and has earned its +10 pp on the NGSA since then. There is nothing to decide, and it is never called the next generation.
6. Can the suppliers carry it [CX-0613, CX-0633]: hold adds no project and no strain. An Open Fan would put a new compact core and fan on the same hot-section suppliers that carry LEAP kits and shop material (Ali; doctrine).
7. The next generation [CX-0217, CX-0208]: no fuel-burn claim, and no "next generation" wording. The 20% line binds RISE; no RISE product is proposed, so it isn't engaged, and there is nothing to strike or rebut.
8. Tie-break: not needed. Hold leads the next-best row by $13.22B, far outside the $1B ε.
9. Premium cap (H9): $0 this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game.

EXCO, UNDER THE TEAM RULE
I proposed hold, and both colleagues recommend hold on every field.
- Ghai's binding vetoes are all conditional or standing, and none is triggered:
  - an Open Fan, alone or with Lobby;
  - Lobby alone;
  - Embraer spend or numbers before a volume is agreed;
  - price, rate, capacity or volume talk without Safran, which includes repeating Airbus's range, a CFM slice of it, or the A320neo slots coming back.
  The statement passes his terms test, and I used his wording for the Airbus extension.
- Ali's date veto is conditional and not triggered: every value rests on the board's development times (2041, 2042, 2060), and no public line or public move carries a year.
- Ali raises no safety or durability flag.
- So I have no failed test to answer, and overrides is empty.

STRAIN READING (re-tied, inference)
- Ghai's model ties the rows with no new strain: $5.96B plus $8B gives -13.96, and $4.21B plus $9B gives -13.21, against the grid's -13.97 and -13.22.
- With $2B of strain the rows would read -15.97 and -15.22, and neither ties. So the bills are $8B and $9B.
- The Board's $11B reading changes no call.
- Ali: on the shop floor there is one hardware project, and Lobby loads no supplier.

SAFRAN GATE (H7) [CX-0184, CX-0166]
- open_fan (hold): RISE stays the 50-50 technology programme. We ask Safran to fund no product that no airframer can take inside the window, and holding asks nothing of the partner.
- lobby_emissions (hold): it serves RISE and is not proposed without an Open Fan, so nothing goes to Safran.
- ducted (hold): it is ready, a defence of the installed base both partners share. No new order.
- partner_embraer (hold): no new order. Anything that goes to Embraer goes to Safran first.
- The Airbus long-term supply answer stays joint, with price, rate and capacity to Safran first. Safran agrees the public acknowledgement's wording first.
- LEAP kits and shop-visit material are CFM practice with Safran.
- genx: GE alone, no gate.

RECONCILIATION (candid, in numbers)
- Round 3 forecast S1 -28.04, S2 -27.95, weighted -28.02. Boeing held, so S1 happened, and today's row is -28.04: it held to the cent. The -0.02 against the weighted figure is the S2 weight that didn't happen.

- Book against row: -30.15 against -28.04. The $2.11B gap is Embraer's in-row value, held out by rule until a volume is agreed. That is the rule working, not a forecast error.

AIRBUS EXTENSION (Ghai's volumes-first test)

  - 2,612 is exactly 2049's NGSA engines;
  - the row implies 2,573-2,701 a year in 2050-56, with a CFM slice of 694-729 (723 in 2050).

WHAT WE KNOW AND WHAT WE DON'T
- What we know: deliveries. Every year from 2045 to 2049 ties, and nothing on the record shows an aircraft waiting on a CFM engine.
- The drop below 50% comes mainly from the MAX, our sole-source slot: Boeing deliveries fell from 684 to 483. Ali reads that as the demand side, since Boeing's waiting backlog runs to zero (inference). We keep that private and make no comment on Boeing.
- What we don't know: all five field-data items are open. In 2035 we told the Board it would have numbers by 2045, and in 2050 we still don't. That's a miss, and I own it. None of this changes a hold. Nothing closes because the calendar runs out.

WHAT THE CASE LEAVES OUT (Ghai's rough figures; inference)
- Further MAX decline: 10% fewer is about -0.70.
- Airframer delivery slowdowns: 5% fewer is about -0.65, 10% about -1.29.
- A widebody Re-engine undoing the GEnx step: about -0.23.
- Tariffs and recession.
- Any durability reserve, booked when the need is found.

**What would change the lean.** Nothing on the sheet can change. Only the moves and the statement can:

**Proposed disclosure (draft).** "Control what you can control. The hard part first. A large GTF fleet on the A320neo is coming through the shops, and until every one of those engines flies in the latest configuration, that fleet is not where our customers need it to be. We own that. The fleet's spare parts and shop material come ahead of new-engine deliveries, and we continue the GTF Advantage hot-section kit at standard terms. We report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration, when the data are there to report. The Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine grew out of our next-generation geared turbofan. It has been ready since 2036 and has flown on the new Airbus single-aisle since 2037, alongside CFM. We report its durability as the fleet data show it, by operating environment, hot and sandy included, and claim no more than that. If the data tell us something we don't like, you will hear it from us first. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. The Joint Venture's terms stand as published: risk, investment and revenue are shared, and our gear and our core stay ours. The competition is strong, and we answer it with time on wing and with product, not with price. Our engine is available, as certified, to any new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet, on standard terms, priced for value. We are not in the early entry phase. Our capital order doesn't change: the dividend comes first. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours."

cfo.memo:
Low end first. The only legal row is hold/hold: −1.65 in S1 and −1.65 in S2. Expected −1.65 on any weights; mine are S1 0.75, S2 0.25. We book S1.

Capitalise ends not met by 1.65, final and unchanged since 2045. Whole life on the board's convention: +0.35 of engine value for $2.00B of R&D; about −0.74 discounted. My PV check is +0.374: −0.146 realised in 2037-49, +0.520 still to come in 2050-56. 2045-49 came in exactly as projected. The bridge to 2045 is nil in S1 and +0.03 in S2, because an fps launched now enters service in 2057 or 2060, after the 2056 count.

Do Nothing was never really zero. Once NGSA launched with us, the 2030 hold row stood at −19.49, and cancel in 2035 at −18.62. The $2B was franchise defence. It still missed the objective's test; I won't dress that up.

Cash: $0 new R&D, no write-off. The dividend is covered, debt is on its pre-ASR path, and the stretch was never used.

An fps code is worth 0.00 here, so we pay nothing for it. My ground-3 veto on any concession stands, recorded privately.

Plainly, I missed the 2045 leak at my own veto check: I read the statement, not the public moves. Two more lines leaked: 'changes no payoff on the board' and the Finance-to-Board step. Now I've read every public line.

It's my job to always worry about things. The one the grid doesn't carry: 13 years with no durability data.

ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ORDERS: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. These are the only values the brief lists (round4.md §3). The grid has one row: −1.65 in S1 and −1.65 in S2.

WHY `gtf2_solo: hold`. GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture when it formed in 2035. Its engine is the Joint Venture engine: ready since 2036, on NGSA since 2037. It has no separate order, cancel or `launch_if_selected` left. Hold keeps the one in-service engine and its durability work whole.

WHY `jv_with_rr: hold`. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and withdrawal is possible only before formation (rules.md). Hold keeps it on its published terms: one engine, the gear and core P&W's work-share and IP [P-1233], and partner content only as an engineering change with its own test evidence.

ANSWERS TO CALIO

(1) Proposal: as above. Holding costs nothing technically. The tie-break agrees: the fleet beats a new engine.

(2) Readiness: confirmed.
- Ready = min(formation 2035 + 6 = 2041; GTF2 2030 + 6 = 2036; UltraFan NB 2030 + 7 = 2037) = 2036.
- NGSA: EIS 2037, code 7, CFM + PW + RR fitted, a 1-year margin. No live airframe is waiting for EIS.
- A 2050 fps would enter service in 2057 on a 7-yr launch (21-year margin), or in 2060 on a 10-yr launch or via Embraer (24 years). S2 is the 2060 case.
- No second development is running, and new R&D is $0.
- Any fps-specific rating, installation or derivative change is an engineering change with its own severe-environment test evidence, not a promise.
- Caution on myself: the board sets ready at launch + 6 and models no slip. The 2036 date held by rule, which is not proof that our dates stopped slipping (Advantage: mid-2024 became 2025 [PX-0128][P-0785]).

(3) In-service durability, the bad number first. After 13 years on NGSA (2037-49), the brief and our files hold none of these:
- time-on-wing figures;
- LLP life against plan, by part family;
- shop-visit findings by cause;
- removal rates;
- hot-and-sandy fleet-leader data;
- the 2036 gate data (which the Board asked for in round 2);
- evidence that the LLPs were at full life at the 2037 EIS.
I invent none. That gap is what goes first to the Governance and Public Policy Committee. No news is not good news: I said "there's not a surprise here coming" five weeks before the 2023 recall [PX-0112][PX-0290]. The method stays: report by operating environment, never as a fleet average. In 2023 three quarters of the fleet flew cool, and that hid the hot-and-sandy shortfall [PX-0122]. Report LLP life against the life declared at EIS [PX-0128].

(4) Parts and capacity to 2056: ground 2 PASSES.
- OE load (brief §1): 978, 987, 982, 947, 938, 950 and 955 engines in 2050-56. The peak, 987 in 2051, is 3.6% under the 2044 peak of 1,024.
- Steps: +2.5% (2050), +0.9% (2051), +1.3% (2055) and +0.5% (2056). Each is small against the +40% ramp of 2040-44.
- The 2045-49 deliveries came in as projected (976, 968, 976, 928, 954).
- Installed base on the board's counts: 7,339 engines in 2026-36, 18,739 in 2026-49, and 25,476 by 2056.
- Limits of the board: it counts P&W's share. The split between A320neo GTF and the Joint Venture engine, and between our shops and Rolls-Royce's, is not in my brief. The board models no shop visits, so I give no dated shop-visit peak.
- OE pull is easing. Airbus's NGSA long-term agreements run at 2,612-2,732 engines a year, 1.4-5.7% below 2044's 2,770, and A320neo slots end with the last aircraft. GTF pacing parts move to MRO.
- Ranking on the roughly 30 pacing parts [PX-0123]: AOG spares, then shop material [PX-0124], then kit parts, then OE. It is decided daily and reviewed weekly [PX-0131].
- A supplier quality gate comes before each rate step, including each NGSA long-term-agreement step, because the powder-metal escape came from a ramp [P-1040].
- The brief shows no live escape.

(5) Configuration control. The rule is confirmed: partner content enters only after EIS, as an engineering change with its own test evidence, and P&W signs durability only on what it tested [P-1215]. Nothing on the record shows otherwise. There is no new programme and $0 of R&D, and Rolls-Royce's 2045 and 2050 lines give no date for any of its content entering the engine. The engineering-change log itself is not in my brief, so I confirm the rule and the record, not the log. The log goes to the committee. The gear and core stay P&W's [P-1233].

(6) GTF Advantage kit.
- It continues at standard terms with pass-through pricing [PX-0117] (applying this to the kit is inference).
- No fleet-configuration share exists after 60% in June 2023, against a target of 90% in 2-3 years [PX-0116] with no outcome on the record. We publish none.
- The 'not where customers need it to be' line rests on one thing we can show: the kit programme continues, so part of the fleet is not yet in the latest configuration. We have no AOG figure after 10% in June 2023 [PX-0120].
- Your new conditional wording ('until every one of those engines flies in the latest configuration') rests on exactly that and invents no figure either way. PASS.

(7) Test 3: CONTINUE through 2056. My call. Conditions:
- (a) time on wing ahead of fuel burn, with no new programme and no board R&D;
- (b) each change goes in with its own severe-environment test evidence;
- (c) kit parts rank behind AOG spares and shop material;
- (d) the in-service team that works the shop findings does the work;
- plus Neil's condition: inside the existing budget, with anything above it going to his gate.
Two more: point the work at shop findings by cause, and report its effect by operating environment. If it pulls engineers or pacing parts from the shops, we drop it. The game ends; the fleet does not.

(8) Statement and public moves, now, not at the veto step. All PASS my two grounds. Advice, not binding:
- 'We report its durability as the fleet data show it' should become 'We claim no more for its durability than the fleet data show, by operating environment, hot and sandy included.' We have reported nothing in 13 years. Present tense reads as reassurance.
- 'Learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF' is your line [PX-0073]. Its lesson, time on wing and LLP life out of the box, is exactly the data we lack. That is fine only beside the line above.
- Public move 1 (Advantage): strip 'changes no payoff on the board', the evidence-file wording and the bracketed ids.
- Public move 4 (JV terms): strip 'through Finance to the full Board before signature', a governance step, into a private note.
- Public move 5: keep 'as certified' and the engineering-change sentence; strip any veto or grid text.
- Both stripped sentences (moves 1 and 4) also leaked in 2045.

(9) Ground 1 PASSES and ground 2 PASSES. No veto.

ops.memo:
The bad number first. Our Joint Venture engine has flown on NGSA for 13 years, 2037 to 2049, and I can't put one time-on-wing, LLP-life or shop-visit figure in front of the Governance and Public Policy Committee. They're not in my brief or our files. I won't make one up, and I won't read no news as good news. I said "there's not a surprise here coming" once, five weeks before a recall.

What I can confirm. One engine: the folded GTF2, launched 2030, ready 2036, on NGSA since 2037. No second development, $0 new R&D. As certified it meets any fps EIS from a 2050 launch, 2057 or 2060. Gear and core stay ours. The change log goes to the committee.

Parts. OE runs 938 to 987 engines a year to 2056, 3.6% under the 2044 peak; biggest step +2.5%. About 18,700 counted P&W engines since 2026 are coming through the shops. Pacing parts: AOG, shop material, kits, then OE, daily, with quality gates before each step. No live escape in the brief. Ground 2 passes.

I propose hold and hold, the only legal values. No veto. Keep the time-on-wing work to 2056 on the four conditions. The game ends; the fleet doesn't.

One line to fix now: "We report its durability" becomes "We claim no more for its durability than the fleet data show." We haven't reported any.

My record is one event, June 2023. The in-service views are seat doctrine.

other_moves.move: GTF Advantage hot-section durability kit across the A320neo fleet
other_moves.detail: We keep fitting the hot-section kit to the in-service A320neo GTF fleet at standard terms with pass-through pricing. There is no free upgrade and no launch-style discount. We report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration, and we publish that share only when we have the data to support it. We give no dated recovery. The fleet's spare parts and shop material come ahead of kit parts.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture held to its published terms
other_moves.detail: The terms are the ones published with the 2035 commitment. Risk, investment and revenue are shared, and both partners are on one engine. The gear and the core stay Pratt & Whitney's work-share and intellectual property. Partner contributions are recognised only in the share split, with no licence and no cash payment to the partner. Partner content enters the certified engine only as an engineering change with its own test evidence, and Pratt & Whitney signs for durability only on an engine it has tested.

decision.public_statement:
Control what you can control. The hard part first. A large GTF fleet on the A320neo is coming through the shops, and until every one of those engines flies in the latest configuration, that fleet is not where our customers need it to be. We own that. The fleet's spare parts and shop material come ahead of new-engine deliveries, and we are continuing the GTF Advantage hot-section kit at standard terms. We will report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration when we have the data to report it.

The Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine grew out of our next-generation geared turbofan. It has been ready since 2036 and has flown on the new Airbus single-aisle since 2037, alongside CFM. We claim no more for its durability than the fleet data show, and we will report those data by operating environment, hot and sandy included. If the data tell us something we don't like, you will hear it from us first. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

The competition is strong, and it should be. We answer it with time on wing and with product, not with price. The Joint Venture's terms stand as published: risk, investment and revenue are shared, and our gear and our core stay ours, in work-share and in intellectual property.

Our engine is available, as certified, to any new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet, on standard terms, priced for value. Any change a new airframe needs goes in with its own test evidence. We are not in the early entry phase. Our capital order doesn't change: the dividend comes first. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours.
decision.rationale:
**Decision.** `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`.
- Eddy proposed both. They are the only legal values (brief §3), and neither is a Board item.
- Grid row 'GTF2: hold': −1.65 in S1 and −1.65 in S2.
- Predictions: S1 0.75, S2 0.25. These are Mitchill's weights; I drop my +0.05 toward S2. His point stands: the MAX shortfall and the backlog reaching 0 by 2050 were already in Boeing's own 2045 numbers, and Boeing again says it is not launching this year and gives no date. The weights move no dollar. Expected column: S1.
- `expected_pv_b` −1.65 on any weights. Worst column: either, at −1.65.
- `premium_b` 0, and `overrides` empty.

**Constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073].**
- Readiness. The Joint Venture engine is the folded GTF2. Its ready year is min(2041, 2036, 2037) = 2036, against NGSA's EIS of 2037. No live airframe is waiting for EIS.
- Any 2050 fps would enter service in 2057 or 2060. The engine meets that as certified, and any airframe-specific change goes in as an engineering change with its own test evidence.
- The bad number: after 13 years in service (2037-49) we hold no time-on-wing, LLP-life, shop-visit, removal or hot-and-sandy figures, no 2036 gate data, and no evidence that the LLPs were at full life at EIS. That gap goes first to the Governance and Public Policy Committee, and we invent nothing.
- Eddy notes, and I agree, that the 2036 date held by rule, not by proof. My own operating dates have slipped before [PX-0017][PX-0098].

**Tests.**
- Visible demand and miss a cycle: nothing to bite on. We are on NGSA, and any fps code now lands after the 2056 count. 'Miss a cycle' was said of RTX's businesses in general [PX-0071], so applying it to engines is inference.
- Responsible bet: no capital order, and $0 of new R&D.
- Dividend safe: confirmed by Mitchill.
- Value, not share: S2 − S1 = 0.00, so we pay nothing.
- Objective: credibility MET; capitalise NOT MET by 1.65, final.

**ExCo veto checks.**
- Mitchill, ground 1 (dividend and debt): not applicable. The envelope passes, the dividend is covered, debt is on its pre-ASR path, and the stretch was unused across the game.
- Mitchill, ground 2 (unselected engine): not applicable. There is no launch or cancel row, and the engine is in service on NGSA code 7.
- Mitchill, ground 3 (aggressive terms): the draft passes. His binding veto on any concession for an fps code or NGSA share is accepted and recorded privately.
- Mitchill, ground 4 (booking upside): passes, with S1 −1.65 booked. His conditional veto is not triggered.
- Eddy, ground 1 (durability before EIS): passes.
- Eddy, ground 2 (parts and capacity): passes. OE runs 938-987 engines a year to 2056, the peak is 3.6% under 2044, the largest step is +2.5%, and the brief shows no live escape. No veto.
- No red-line flag. `overrides` empty.

**Final whole-life review (Mitchill, for Finance).**
- −1.65 = +0.35 − $2.00B. It is −1.65 against Do Nothing and trails a $2.00B buyback by 1.65.
- Discounted: about −0.74.
- PV +0.374: −0.146 realised in 2037-49 (including −1.2, −1.1 and −0.9 nominal in 2038-40) and +0.520 still to come in 2050-56.
- 2045-49 came in exactly as projected.
- Bridge to 2045: nil in S1, and +0.03 in S2 because a 2050 fps enters service after 2056. That is not value created.
- Long view: +0.42 PV for 2057-60, not booked.
- The $2.00B was franchise defence, against a real Do Nothing of −19.49 in 2030. It still fails the objective's test. I won't dress that up.

**Tie-breaks.**
- The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]: pacing parts rank AOG spares, then shop material, then kits, then OE.
- Miss a cycle: not engaged.
- A rival's discount never moves our price [PX-0055].

**Disclosure.**
- I own the 2045 slip. Mitchill found three leaks in that year's public moves.
- In 2050 the public moves and the statement carry no valuation, grid figure, veto, governance step, evidence tag, share projection, airframer date, or EIS for anything new.
- Durability wording follows Eddy: 'claim no more than the fleet data show'.

**Doctrine, not my record.**
- The Joint Venture: I have no evidence of my own, so I take Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test.
- The in-service durability method is Eddy's seat doctrine; his record is one event.
- Visible demand [PX-0109] and miss a cycle [PX-0071] are RTX-wide lines; applying them here is inference.

final.public_statement:
Control what you can control. The hard part first. A large GTF fleet on the A320neo is coming through the shops, and until every one of those engines flies in the latest configuration, that fleet is not where our customers need it to be. We own that. The fleet's spare parts and shop material come ahead of new-engine deliveries, and we are continuing the GTF Advantage hot-section kit at standard terms. We will report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration when we have the data to report it.

The Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine grew out of our next-generation geared turbofan. It has been ready since 2036 and has flown on the new Airbus single-aisle since 2037, alongside CFM. We claim no more for its durability than the fleet data show, and we will report those data by operating environment, hot and sandy included. If the data tell us something we don't like, you will hear it from us first. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

The competition is strong, and it should be. We answer it with time on wing and with product, not with price. The Joint Venture's terms stand as published: risk, investment and revenue are shared, and our gear and our core stay ours, in work-share and in intellectual property.

Our engine is available, as certified, to any new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet, on standard terms, priced for value. Any change a new airframe needs goes in with its own test evidence. We are not in the early entry phase. Our capital order doesn't change: the dividend comes first. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours.
