recommendations.text:
Hold both widebody items. Defend the franchise through time on wing.
- The franchise test is not triggered: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 55.2% in 2050 (58.0% in S4), and no rival-engined Re-engine is on the record.
- Keep Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 durability inside the existing budget (the about £1bn programme), and keep watching Boeing's 787 work with GE.
- Beyond this game's horizon, the doctrine stands: a widebody programme comes to the Board only with a Re-engine on the record, and only if it pays after the cost of running two programmes.

Commercial discipline. Narrowbody is an option, not a need, and it carries no premium.
- S2 equals S1 on the hold row: a Boeing fps selection adds nothing on this board.
- Keep the Joint Venture engine on offer to any new single-aisle on standard terms, through the Investment Committee: no price concessions, no dates, no launch-style terms.
- Our answer to any doubt on readiness is in-service durability data.

Make the Joint Venture work on aligned terms. That is the IAE lesson.
- Keep one engineering interface and one durability standard with P&W.
- Keep one chief engineer per change, and credit each change as a valuation in the share split only.
- Add our partner shops to P&W's network rather than replacing it.
- P&W says its own GTF fleet is still not where customers need it, so durability is a shared exposure.
- Bring any Joint Venture share or term question to the Board before it is public.

Capacity and support for the ramp.
- The narrowbody line runs at about 930-990 engines a year to 2060, against 188 widebody.
- The support network must cover about 8,848 Rolls-Royce engines by the end of 2050 and about 14,600 by 2056 (brief §1 sums).
- Keep Trent XWB and Trent 7000 supply, spares and support ring-fenced, with ring-fence status reported alongside the fleet report.
- Ration engineering changes, fleet first.

frame.question:
So, 2050. This is the last round. The question is the quality of earnings and cash on the engine we already fly, not share [RX-0054]. There is nothing left to win on the grid. There is a lot left to lose.
- The Joint Venture engine with P&W has been in service on NGSA since 2037. On the brief's §1 sums Rolls-Royce has about 7,870 narrowbody engines delivered by end-2049, about 8,848 by end-2050 and about 14,600 by 2056. Deliveries run at 930-990 a year, against 188 widebody engines a year.
- The aftermarket cash on that fleet depends on time on wing, shop visits and support. "I worry about tomorrow's financials" [RX-0125].

Three questions, in this order:
(1) Delivery. Is the Joint Venture fleet run to the written durability standard, with support scaled to about 8,848 engines and Trent XWB and Trent 7000 ring-fenced? Both narrowbody fields can only be held, so this is the real job.
(2) Widebody money. Does any of it move in the final round? I say no.
- The Joint Venture is ready and cannot be cancelled, so the $5B strain on any widebody item is permanent.
- No round follows this one, so a launch now cannot be cancelled. The full bill and the strain land.
- Against hold, the Trent 1000 upgrade is -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.62 and UltraFan WB is -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.68 / -8.32. Each loses more than its own bill in every column.
(3) Close-out. Each of the Board's round-3 recommendations gets an honest final status, and the Audit Committee gets the Joint Venture lookback against the $4B line, which we missed.

"We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically" [RX-0058].

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
On the grid, nothing this round can change it. Either widebody item needs about $5B of engine value just to stay within its own bill, and this board gives at most $0.38B and $0.68B, even in S4 alone. What would move me:
(1) A later grid in which a widebody row beats hold, or falls short by no more than the $3B cap ($1B for UltraFan WB) as a declared premium, with a Re-engine on the record. That lies beyond this game.
(2) Joint Venture in-service data below the written standard on time on wing, shop-visit rate, life-limited parts or aircraft on ground. I would re-price the LTSA balance and the lookback, test for onerous contracts, and say so first, with P&W. Safety comes first.
(3) Free cash flow well below guidance. I would revisit the pace of distributions, not support or safety spend.
(4) Concessions, dates or launch-style terms added as other moves. I would withhold my support.
(5) Delivered NGSA pricing and shop-visit data in place of the board's 1.6x lifecycle multiple. That would move the lookback IRR either way; today's 9-12% is a floor.
cfo.memo:
Safety, then the balance sheet. This is the last round, and a delivery round.

I confirm Tufan's grid. Hold is +11.03 / +11.03 / +11.03 / +11.37: +11.05 on his weights and the Board's, +11.10 on the Re-engine stress. Against hold, the Trent 1000 upgrade is −6.73 / −6.73 / −6.73 / −6.62, or −6.72 expected. UltraFan WB is −9.00 / −9.00 / −8.68 / −8.32, or −8.93. Each loses more than its own bill in every column: the $5B strain is permanent beside the Joint Venture, and no later round can cancel. My 2045 estimate held for the upgrade; for UltraFan WB, my −8.6 was the Re-engine case, and the expected figure is 0.3 worse. Nothing on this board passes. I withhold my signature on both.

No new programme spend. No equity, no new borrowing, leverage unchanged. Payout stays at 30-40%; buybacks on fit, value and timing, never on borrowed money. Narrowbody cash is booked as delivered.

The lookback, plainly. We spent $5.71B against a $4B line: missed, beyond repair. Delivered share is 26.4% in 2050; nothing in our position has moved since 2045. On Civil margins of 17-25%, the return is about 9-12%, below our mid-to-high teens. It adds value; it does not clear the hurdle. Hold that as a floor: my record on launch economics is thin.

The job now is the quality of cash: time on wing, shop visits, support.

That's how you should hold it. That's our best view at the minute.

tests.name: Ready by EIS

A late engine fails as advice: it is not fitted, and McCabe prices the downside. A late engine is not a veto ground.

Widebody (for the record; I hold both):
- Trent 1000 upgrade launched 2050: it counts from 2053 (2050 + 3), giving 9 counting years to 2061, in every column.
- UltraFan WB launched 2050: ready 2056 (2050 + 6). The earliest Re-engine EIS is 2055 (2050 + 5, in S3-S4), so UltraFan WB would be a year late for it. That is a fail as advice, had it been launched. It would count 2056-2061 in S3-S4 only and earns nothing in S1-S2.
- Engine value each buys (its row against hold, plus its bill and the $5B strain): upgrade $0.27B / $0.27B / $0.27B / $0.38B; UltraFan WB $0 / $0 / $0.32B / $0.68B.

tests.name: No early date
tests.numbers:
I read the CEO's draft statement word by word. It contains no year and no number.
- 'in service on NGSA, and we pace it on durability': a fact on the record, with no date.
- 'Support through our partner shops, alongside Pratt & Whitney's network, scales with the fleet': no date, and true as a plan. The private move sizes it for about 8,850 engines by end-2050. The brief carries no MRO capacity figure, so it stays a plan statement, not a completion claim.

- 'If the in-service data tell us something we don't like, we will say so first': keep it. P&W says the same.
- 'comes to the Board only once a Re-engine is on the record, and only if it pays after the cost of running two programmes': conditional, with no date.
- The statement says nothing on Airbus's or Boeing's dates or rates. 'We are not after market share' is not a share claim.

Option E public moves (i)-(iii) carry no year: (i) 'with no date'; (ii) 'no dates'; (iii) Trent durability inside the existing budget.

Drafting advice only, not a Civil ground. Move (iii) closes with 'No grid adjustment'. That is board language, not a number. I would keep it in the private record, consistent with the round-3 note. The '£1bn programme' is a company budget figure, not a grid number, and it can stay.

tests.numbers:
NGSA (EIS 2037): the plan was live before EIS. It had Singapore-model partner shops with repair technology, a spares and lease-engine pool, and an EIS field team.

Cumulative Rolls-Royce narrowbody fleet (my sums of brief §1):
- 4,044 by end-2045; 5,012 (2046); 5,988 (2047); 6,916 (2048); 7,870 (2049); 8,848 (2050);
- 9,835 (2051); 11,764 (2053); 13,652 (2055); 14,607 (2056); 18,381 (2060).

Sizing:
- The round-3 private move scales the network to about 8,850 engines by end-2050. That matches 8,848.
- The next step is about 14,600 by 2056: 5,759 more engines, about 960 a year. That is +65% on the 2050 network.
- The fleet keeps growing after the board's count ends, to about 18,400 by 2060.
- P&W holds an equal Joint Venture share, so the NGSA Joint Venture fleet is larger than ours (inference). Our shops add to P&W's network; they do not replace it.
- The spares and lease pool and the field team scale with deliveries. Spares go to aircraft on ground first.

A new single-aisle: the earliest EIS is 2057 (a 7-year fps launched in 2050) or 2060 (10-year). The same network would be extended before that EIS.

What I cannot confirm: the brief has no MRO capacity or shop-visit data. I use my CMD figure of 1,100-1,200 shop visits a year (RX-0279). It is a widebody-era number, never reconciled with Helen's 1,400-1,500 (RX-0223), and I set no narrowbody shop-visit rate.

- UltraFan WB: development 2050-56 ($4B, about $0.67B a year over 2050-55), beside 938-987 a year.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection. Time on wing is the lever (inference).

One standard, one fleet report, by operating environment (hot and sandy included), as P&W now publishes.

tests.numbers:

Crediting:

Any of these would change my view:
- **Fleet data below the written standard.** On time on wing, shop-visit rate, life-limited parts or aircraft on ground, we say so first, with P&W. Engineers and spares go to the fleet before anything new.
- **Content rushed into the certified engine.** Any proposal to put Rolls-Royce content in to hold a date or win a selection, without its own test evidence, is compressed maturity. I would invoke the Civil veto, binding.
- **A date in public.** I would invoke the veto for any of these:
  - a date for our content entering the engine;
  - a Joint Venture date other than the bulletin's;
  - an upgrade count before 2053;
  - an UltraFan WB date before 2056.
- **A capacity or MRO constraint in the brief.** It would make the capacity test live, and I would ask for the support build to 14,600 engines by 2056 to be re-sized before anything else.
- **A rival-engined 787 Re-engine on the record, or a brief projecting our widebody share near 50%.** Either would trigger the franchise test, with time on wing as the first lever. On this board, any widebody item still needs about $5B of engine value just to cover the permanent strain.
- **Named airline wins and in-service data.** These firm up my confidence in the support ramp. Wins on the Joint Venture engine and time-on-wing data inside the specification would both count.
ops.memo:
All four fields at hold. No Civil veto: nothing compresses maturity, and nothing public carries a date.

Readiness. The Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036 and has flown on NGSA since 2037, a year of margin. No other airframe awaits an engine.

The fleet. About 7,870 Rolls-Royce engines at end-2049, 8,848 at end-2050 and 14,600 by 2056. The brief gives deliveries, not fleet data. So I report against the written standard (time on wing, shop-visit rate, life-limited parts, aircraft on ground) and invent no figure. One standard and one fleet report with P&W, by operating environment. If the data are bad, operators and Airbus hear it from us and P&W first, then the public, with the fix and no recovery date.

Support. Partner shops on the Singapore model, added to P&W's network. Sized for about 8,850 engines by end-2050, then about 14,600 by 2056.

The rule. Our content goes in only as an engineering change with its own test evidence. One chief engineer per change, fleet first.

Capacity. 978 narrowbody engines against 188 widebody in 2050. No constraint in the brief. Trent XWB and Trent 7000 stay ring-fenced.

Widebody. 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050. The upgrade would count from 2053 and UltraFan WB would be ready in 2056. Each carries a permanent $5B strain: −6.73 and −9.00. Trent durability inside the existing budget does the fleet work.

We're absolutely focused on keeping our engines flying and earning for as long as possible.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture engine in service, paced on durability; engineering-change rule
other_moves.detail: The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on NGSA, and we pace it on durability. Rolls-Royce content enters the certified engine only as an engineering change with its own test evidence. It is never used to hold a date or win a campaign. P&W's published terms say the same. If the in-service data tell us something we don't like, we say so first, with P&W. No date of any kind is given for our content entering the engine [RX-0296, RX-0284, R-1476].

other_moves.move: Joint Venture engine on offer to any new single-aisle, on standard terms
other_moves.detail: The Joint Venture engine is on offer to any new single-aisle on standard 'win-win' terms, through the Investment Committee: no price concessions, no dates, no launch-style terms. Our answer to any doubt on readiness is in-service durability data. We are not after market share [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582].

other_moves.move: Trent durability and UltraFan technology pull-through inside the existing budget
other_moves.detail: Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 HP turbine and life-limited-part durability work continues inside the existing durability budget (the about £1bn programme). UltraFan demonstrator technology, and the technology from the folded UltraFan NB, keep flowing into the in-service Trent fleet for time on wing, inside a broadly flat gross R&D envelope. This is not a Trent upgrade programme [RX-0123, RX-0214].

other_moves.move: Joint Venture governance with P&W (the IAE lesson)
Fleet report to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee against the written standard
Joint Venture support network scaled to the fleet

The network is sized for about 8,850 Rolls-Royce engines by end-2050 and is planned to reach about 14,600 by 2056 (about +65%, roughly 960 engines a year), with the fleet growing to about 18,400 by 2060. Support commitments go through the Investment Committee and are funded inside the Civil operating budget [RX-0283, RX-0287].

other_moves.move: Supplier and capacity plan; widebody ring-fence
other_moves.detail: Trent XWB and Trent 7000 supply, spares and support stay ring-fenced, and ring-fence status is reported alongside the fleet report. Castings and forgings go with high-performing suppliers. Gearbox and shop capacity are shared with P&W under its terms. In 2050 we deliver about 978 narrowbody engines against 188 widebody, and the brief reports no constraint [RX-0284, RX-0286].

other_moves.move: Capital frame and final Joint Venture lookback to the Audit Committee
Widebody doctrine beyond the game horizon; watch on Boeing's 787 work with GE
other_moves.detail: To the Board only. A widebody programme comes to the Board only with a 787 or A350 Re-engine on the public record, and only if it pays after the cost of running two programmes. On this board each item needs about $5B of engine value just to cover the strain. Neither is an option we keep warm [RX-0051, R-1573, R-1574]. We keep watching Boeing's 787 work with GE: today it is 'not a 787 Re-engine order', and the GEnx upgrade is already inside our 55.2%.

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on NGSA, and we pace it on durability. Our job is to deliver what flies: time on wing, support, durability. Support through our partner shops, alongside Pratt & Whitney's network, scales with the fleet. Any Rolls-Royce content that enters that engine goes in as an engineering change with its own test evidence. We don't compress it for anyone. If the in-service data tell us something we don't like, we will say so first. The engine is on offer to any new single-aisle on standard terms. Widebody is our core. Our Trent durability work continues inside our existing budget. Any UltraFan widebody or Trent upgrade comes to the Board only once a Re-engine is on the record, and only if it pays after the cost of running two programmes. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
So, the last round. All four fields at hold. The work this round is delivery, not launches.

1. START FROM MY PROPOSAL. I framed all four fields at hold. Both memos recommend the same orders, and neither raises a binding veto against them.
- ultrafan_nb_solo: hold. The Solo was folded in 2035, and hold is the only legal value.
- jv_with_pw: hold. The Joint Venture is formed, ready since 2036 and in service. Hold keeps it as approved, and it is the only legal value.
- ultrafan_wb: hold.
- t1000_upgrade: hold.

2. GRID ROWS, with and without each item (brief §3, S1-S4). Weights are mine, since the brief gives none: 0.75 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05.
- Hold: +11.03 / +11.03 / +11.03 / +11.37. Expected +11.05 on my weights and on the Board's (0.80 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.05), +11.10 on the Re-engine stress (0.40 / 0.10 / 0.30 / 0.20), +11.37 on S4 alone. Worst column +11.03. It is the best plan in every column.
- Hold + T1000 upgrade: +4.30 / +4.30 / +4.30 / +4.75. Against hold that is -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.62: -6.72 expected on my weights and the Board's, -6.71 on the stress, -6.62 on S4. Worst column -6.73, beyond its own -$2B bill. It buys about $0.27B of engine value ($0.38B in S4) for $2B of bill plus the permanent $5B strain.
- Hold + UltraFan WB: +2.03 / +2.03 / +2.35 / +3.05. Against hold that is -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.68 / -8.32: -8.93 expected on my weights and the Board's, -8.77 on the stress, -8.32 on S4. Worst column -9.00, beyond its own -$4B bill. It is ready in 2056, a year after the earliest Re-engine EIS (2055), and buys $0 / $0 / $0.32B / $0.68B for $9B.
Each item has the same sign in every column, so no verdict turns on the weights. No later round exists to cancel either item: the full bill and the strain land. Calculations are in /tmp/wargame-rolls_royce/dash-2050-cons/work/r4_decide_calc.txt.

3. BINDING VETOES. McCabe withholds her co-signature on both widebody launches: binding, and moot, because I propose neither. Watson's Civil veto is not invoked: nothing is compressed, and no public text carries a date. No plan is struck on a veto, because none was proposed. Overrides: empty.

4. MY TESTS.
- Airframers first [RX-0058]: no 787 or A350 Re-engine has been launched or announced. Boeing calls its GE work 'not a 787 Re-engine order', and Airbus keeps the A350 as its focus. UltraFan WB has no airframe to fly.
- Four-part gate [RX-0030]: both items fail 'viable business model' on the strain, and UltraFan WB also fails 'large market'.
- Profitable or not at all: both are negative in every column. 'We won't do anything not profitable' [RX-0058].
- Widebody franchise: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 (58.0% in S4). The 50% line is not threatened, so no premium is triggered.
- Premium cap: the shortfalls are $6.72B against the $3B cap and $8.93B against the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap. Both are declined.
- No options management [RX-0051]: no widebody item launched as a hedge.
- Cash as an input [RX-0042]: McCabe's capex (about £0.49bn a year for either item) and the downside were on the table before I chose. The package spends £0.
- On 787 share I said 'Why not?' [RX-0117]. On this board the answer is $6.7B. 'We are not after market share' [R-1582].

5. EXPECTED SCENARIO: S1. Boeing launches nothing and gives no date, there is no Re-engine, and CFM/GE launches no new programme. The best grid plan in S1, and in every other column, is all hold. Premium 0.

6. RED-LINE CHECK BEFORE RETURNING. All hold breaks no company red line.
- McCabe flagged that UltraFan WB with no Re-engine on the record would breach 'no UltraFan launch without an airframe to fly it'. I confirm the flag. It is struck by holding: no launch.
- Watson flagged 'No grid adjustment' in public move (iii) as board language. I take that: the phrase is removed from the public text. Last round's public move (ii) carried a grid figure (S2 against S1). This round's public text carries none.
- The public statement is Watson-checked word for word: no dates, nothing on Airbus's or Boeing's dates or rates, no share claim, and the widebody line conditional.
- No flag is left unresolved.

7. BOARD. No order differs from the default, so there is no Board item. Every guidance point is answered in board_response, with a final status for each round-3 recommendation.

8. WHERE THIS IS DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD. I have no evidenced decision on running a formed Joint Venture. The governance, fleet-report, support and lookback moves follow company doctrine (profile.md §4, §9 steps 6-12), Watson's attributed maturity rule and the Board's guidance. The capital frame and the lookback are McCabe's evidence. On the lookback I take her number plainly: 9-12% does not clear the mid-to-high teens. It adds value. It is not good enough by our own hurdle [RX-0033], and I say so to the Audit Committee.

'They are a milestone on our journey, not our final destination' [RX-0062].

- She confirms the grid line by line: hold +11.05 expected, upgrade -6.72, UltraFan WB -8.93, and the decomposition ($0.27-0.38B and $0-0.68B of engine value against $7B and $9B).
- She withholds her co-signature on both widebody launches. That is binding, and moot on all-hold.

- Her 2045 estimate held for the upgrade. For UltraFan WB it was 0.3 optimistic on expected value, because her -8.6 was the Re-engine case. She said so herself; noted.

- I also take her proposal to carry Joint Venture aftermarket quality (LTSA balance, onerous-contract test) as a standing Audit Committee item. I've seen this movie before: onerous contracts were part of what I inherited [RX-0049].

- Enter narrowbody: MET. Rolls-Royce narrowbody engine share is 23.6% in 2045 and 26.4% in 2050, through the Joint Venture with P&W on NGSA.
- Keep widebody dominance: MET. 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 55.2% in 2050 (58.0% in 2050 in S4). The worst year is 5.2 points above the 50% line.

- Widebody never starved: MET at $0 strain. It holds only because both widebody fields stay at hold, and it is preserved by this round's orders.

final.rationale:
So, the last round. All four fields at hold. The work this round is delivery, not launches.

1. START FROM MY PROPOSAL. I framed all four fields at hold. Both memos recommend the same orders, and neither raises a binding veto against them.
- ultrafan_nb_solo: hold. The Solo was folded in 2035, and hold is the only legal value.
- jv_with_pw: hold. The Joint Venture is formed, ready since 2036 and in service. Hold keeps it as approved, and it is the only legal value.
- ultrafan_wb: hold.
- t1000_upgrade: hold.

2. GRID ROWS, with and without each item (brief §3, S1-S4). Weights are mine, since the brief gives none: 0.75 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05.
- Hold: +11.03 / +11.03 / +11.03 / +11.37. Expected +11.05 on my weights and on the Board's (0.80 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.05), +11.10 on the Re-engine stress (0.40 / 0.10 / 0.30 / 0.20), +11.37 on S4 alone. Worst column +11.03. It is the best plan in every column.
- Hold + T1000 upgrade: +4.30 / +4.30 / +4.30 / +4.75. Against hold that is -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.62: -6.72 expected on my weights and the Board's, -6.71 on the stress, -6.62 on S4. Worst column -6.73, beyond its own -$2B bill. It buys about $0.27B of engine value ($0.38B in S4) for $2B of bill plus the permanent $5B strain.
- Hold + UltraFan WB: +2.03 / +2.03 / +2.35 / +3.05. Against hold that is -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.68 / -8.32: -8.93 expected on my weights and the Board's, -8.77 on the stress, -8.32 on S4. Worst column -9.00, beyond its own -$4B bill. It is ready in 2056, a year after the earliest Re-engine EIS (2055), and buys $0 / $0 / $0.32B / $0.68B for $9B.
Each item has the same sign in every column, so no verdict turns on the weights. No later round exists to cancel either item: the full bill and the strain land. Calculations are in /tmp/wargame-rolls_royce/dash-2050-cons/work/r4_decide_calc.txt.

3. BINDING VETOES. McCabe withholds her co-signature on both widebody launches: binding, and moot, because I propose neither. Watson's Civil veto is not invoked: nothing is compressed, and no public text carries a date. No plan is struck on a veto, because none was proposed. Overrides: empty.

4. MY TESTS.
- Airframers first [RX-0058]: no 787 or A350 Re-engine has been launched or announced. Boeing calls its GE work 'not a 787 Re-engine order', and Airbus keeps the A350 as its focus. UltraFan WB has no airframe to fly.
- Four-part gate [RX-0030]: both items fail 'viable business model' on the strain, and UltraFan WB also fails 'large market'.
- Profitable or not at all: both are negative in every column. 'We won't do anything not profitable' [RX-0058].
- Widebody franchise: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 (58.0% in S4). The 50% line is not threatened, so no premium is triggered.
- Premium cap: the shortfalls are $6.72B against the $3B cap and $8.93B against the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap. Both are declined.
- No options management [RX-0051]: no widebody item launched as a hedge.
- Cash as an input [RX-0042]: McCabe's capex (about £0.49bn a year for either item) and the downside were on the table before I chose. The package spends £0.
- On 787 share I said 'Why not?' [RX-0117]. On this board the answer is $6.7B. 'We are not after market share' [R-1582].

5. EXPECTED SCENARIO: S1. Boeing launches nothing and gives no date, there is no Re-engine, and CFM/GE launches no new programme. The best grid plan in S1, and in every other column, is all hold. Premium 0.

6. RED-LINE CHECK BEFORE RETURNING. All hold breaks no company red line.
- McCabe flagged that UltraFan WB with no Re-engine on the record would breach 'no UltraFan launch without an airframe to fly it'. I confirm the flag. It is struck by holding: no launch.
- Watson flagged 'No grid adjustment' in public move (iii) as board language. I take that: the phrase is removed from the public text. Last round's public move (ii) carried a grid figure (S2 against S1). This round's public text carries none.
- The public statement is Watson-checked word for word: no dates, nothing on Airbus's or Boeing's dates or rates, no share claim, and the widebody line conditional.
- No flag is left unresolved.

7. BOARD. No order differs from the default, so there is no Board item. Every guidance point is answered in board_response, with a final status for each round-3 recommendation.

8. WHERE THIS IS DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD. I have no evidenced decision on running a formed Joint Venture. The governance, fleet-report, support and lookback moves follow company doctrine (profile.md §4, §9 steps 6-12), Watson's attributed maturity rule and the Board's guidance. The capital frame and the lookback are McCabe's evidence. On the lookback I take her number plainly: 9-12% does not clear the mid-to-high teens. It adds value. It is not good enough by our own hurdle [RX-0033], and I say so to the Audit Committee.

'They are a milestone on our journey, not our final destination' [RX-0062].
